speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was notified that this question had been asked1. The question was as follows:
In view of the further increase in the cost of living as reported by the bureau of statistics, what action does the government intend to take to prevent further increases in the cost of at least staple food products, such as milk, meat, butter and bread?
This is a matter, of course, of government policy which will be announced in due course. However, I might point out that the price of milk, for instance, is, and has been for some time, under the control of the provinces. Butter is controlled by a ceiling price at present. I have no indication or information that the price of bread has been increased unduly.
Supply-Agriculture



The house in committee of supply, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

Administration service-
1. Departmental administration, $234,297.

When we went into supply in agriculture on April 27 I asked a few questions of the minister and he intimated that he would give the answers later. Since then I have received other information which I should like to discuss for a moment or two and on the basis of which I will submit one or two more questions which the minister can answer along with those I have already submitted to him.
I have here a journal called Foreign Trade, issued by this government on May 1, 1948, in Ottawa, in which I find an article under the heading:	"Slight improvement indicated
in world food situation this year". This article is by G. R. Paterson, agricultural counsellor, Canadian embassy. It is in the form of a dispatch from Washington on April 8, 1948. I quote:
On January 1, 1948, the international emergency foqd committee of the council of the food and agriculture organization of the united nations assumed the functions of the former international emergency food council in the field of international distribution of foodstuffs and fertilizers continuing in short world supply.
The article points out that there was a slight improvement over last year, which was a very serious year in the matter of foodstuffs throughout the world. I quote further:
Many problems-*
That is, food problems.
Many problems still remain. Rations in some countries have been lower than in the winter of 1946-47 and operating stocks have been less adequate. The gap between available supplies and requirements cannot be wholly closed. While moderate improvement is at present indicated for the period following this year's harvests, nevertheless even the most favourable weather and other conditions would not produce food supplies sufficient to provide pre-war levels of consumption in many countries.
Food shortages in 1948-49 will continue to affect industrial production adversely, to create problems of inflation in many countries and to constitute a continued heavy drain on the foreign exchange resources of many importing countries.
I think that last sentence is significant to agricultural producers in Canada. I raised a question on April 27 with reference to quantities of beef stored in Canada, and having in mind the article from which I have quoted, I should like to repeat-I have said it before

that Canada is the only country

which deliberately channels exports where the producers will not be paid for them. Other countries use controls to send exports where they will be able to secure United States dollars, but the Canadian government does the exact opposite. It imposes embargoes on the shipment of agricultural products to the United States, and it exports to Britain at reduced prices, even though Britain lacks dollars to pay for those exports. Surely this is a mistaken policy, especially wrhen we are the only nation in the world that fosters it. A recent press report indicated that sixty per cent of the $45,000,000 contract figure in respect of beef has been purchased by the meat board for export to the United Kingdom. The year is only one-quarter finished, and our heavy fall marketing period is still ahead of us.
As I have often done in the past, I wish to appeal, with all the eainestness at my command, to the Minister of Agriculture to use his influence with the Minister of l.ade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance to have immediately lifted the embargo against Canadian beef cattle entering our most natural market in the world, the United States. This is tremendously important.
I asked some question about what prospects we had of marketing during this year our agricultural products through the Marshall plan, or what is now known as ERP. According to a press report yesterday, Britain is to get $33,000,000 through this plan in Canada; wheat to the extent of $17,000,000, wheat flour $5,500,000, and bacon $11,000,000. This has been authorized by Paul G. Hoffman, economic administrator of the fund in the United States.
The article in Foreign Trade, issued by the government, to which I have already referred, mentions the possibility of foodstuffs being produced this year under very favourable this country today. I do not think that anyone, judging from past experience, will deny that the wheat producers on the prairies should have their wheat seeded before the 10th of May. It is almost that today, and while we are having difficulties the very opposite of those we experienced in the nineteen thirties- not a dust bowl but extreme flooding even for the prairies-even where flooding has not taken place we have had a tremendous loss up to the present time.
I listened the other morning to an expert who, speaking over the radio, was telling about a survey that had been made, and he said that with favourable conditions from now on, wheat seeding could not become general until

Supply-Agriculture
the middle of May, in the southern part of the prairies, and the end of May in the north. That will be quite late. An exceptional season will be necessary if we are to garner a good wheat harvest, and the weather has not cleared up yet. At the present time, therefore, the prospects for a good wheat harvest are not bright. I am pretty much of an optimist, and I am not yet downhearted about it, because it is marvellous what this country can do in short order. The situation, however, could be a serious one, especially with respect to the marketing of beef. Even the beef producers had great difficulties this spring and are still having difficulties because of the flooding.
Once more I urge the minister to give us a lead as to when the embargo can be lifted from the shipment of beef cattle to the United States, which is by far the best natural market we have in the world. It would mean a good deal to the producers from the standpoint of breeding in the future if they could have some intimation from the minister on that point, and I trust that he will be able to give it to us. I should also like to have him state the figures for meat in storage in the countiy. I asked for that on April 27.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
This, as has been said, is the second meeting of the committee of the whole to consider the estimates on agriculture. Some questions were raised on the previous occasion which I think it would be well to deal with.
The main objective of the questions is, I think, to determine whether we have had an increase or decrease in production in agriculture up to the present time, and as to where we are going from the present position. I believe that in order to arrive at a reasonable conclusion on that question it will be necessary for me to establish the present position in relation to the past on a few of the important products, those that enter most largely into the income which the farmers receive across Canada. I feel that we shall not get very far by dealing with the war years alone. The truth with regard to the war years is that income increased year by year from the beginning until the end of the war, and income is still continuing to increase. Nevertheless we can select individual commodities, such as bacon or butter or cheese, and we can prove certain things with regard to them. Bacon production, for example, increased very rapidly in the early years of the war and decreased in the later years of the war. But when we take the over-all position of production in agriculture and returns from 5849-235
agriculture, there was a gradual increase all the way through the war years. So I think we shall get on the soundest basis for considering the policy for the year 1948 and the years beyond by establishing the position at the end of the war in relation to the position at the beginning of the war so far as production is concerned.
In the first year of the war I stated to the farmers at the time my estimates were going through the house that, in our opinion, the farmers found themselves at the beginning of the war producing most of the commodities that would be required throughout and at the end of the war, and that our efforts ought to be to increase production in certain lines as required, and to establish our industry on a sounder financial basis in order that we might come out of the war in a better position financially than when we went into it. I think the farmers have done that, and I am going to give a few figures which will indicate why I believe so.
If we take the last year before the war, 1939, and compare it with 1946, the first year after the war, we find that milk production was in 1939, 15,781,000,000 and in 1946, 16,936.000,000, an increase of 1,155,000,000 pounds. In other words we came through the war producing more milk than when we went into the war. I am not able to give comparisons in the price of milk for the years before and after the war, for the obvious reason that milk prices vary so much across Canada that it would be impossible to give any one figure which would cover the whole.
In eggs the production in 1939 was 221,000,000 dozen, and in 1946, 316,000,000 dozen, an increase of 95,000,000 dozen. The price in 1939 was 18-5 cents and in 1946, 33-5 cents.
Cattle, slaughtered, in 1939, 1,337,000 head, and in 1946, 2,226,000 head, or an increase of
889,000	head. The price in 1939 was 6-77 cents, and in 1946, 12-52 cents.
Hogs, slaughtered, in 1939, 5,122,000, and in 1946, 7,896,000, an increase of 2,774,000. The price in 1939 of live hogs was 8-85 cents, and in 1946, converted to live weight prices, 14-91 cents.
Barley production in 1939 was 103,000,000 bushels and in 1946 148,000,000 bushels, an increase of 45,000,000 bushels. The price in 1939 was 34 cents and in 1946, 67 cents.
Oats production in 1939 was 384,000,000 bushels, and in 1946, 399,000,000 bushels, an increase of 15,000,000 bushels. The price in 1939 was 30 cents and in 1946, 56 cents.
I have gone over these figures but if the committee will permit me I should like to have the figures, from which I have been quoting, inserted in Hansard in- tabulated form.

Hog storages are a little different. I am told that this figure with respect to pork includes all pork products-bacon, ham and everything of that nature-in storage, wherever it may be stored.

86,000,000?

The actual amounts in storage on April 1 were 26,255,865 pounds for domestic use and 23,204,043 pounds for export. I am told that there is an amount which would be in transfer between one place and another in Canada, but which would not be found in these storage figures. That may bring the amount close to the 86,000,000 mentioned.
I think these figures will give the picture. I would rather have had the figures for May, and while we are discussing the estimates if I find it possible to give those figures I will do so. That would give the complete picture of what has happened since April 1. I believe I have given all the information that was asked for.

I asked about the cost of production, and the minister referred to an earlier statement he had made. I turn to page 3392 of Hansard for April 27, where the minister gave some gross and net figures. I look particularly at the figures for 1946 and 1947. In 1946 the gross income from agricultural production, in round figures, as the minister gave it, was 81,759,000,000, and the net income as he gave it was $1,267,000,000. Then when we come to look at 1947 we find the gross income had gone up by about $455,000,000, the figure being S2,213,900,000. But the net, lower down on the page, is given as $1,259,000,000. What had actually happened was that the net income from 1946 to 1947 had decreased by approximately S8,000,000. The difference, however, in the gross income for the same years was $455,000,000, which means that the cost of production must have gone up by approximately $463,000,000.
I look at the figures for 1938 which the minister gave, and I find he said that in that year the net income of farmers was $387,000,000. The difference which I have indicated, approximately $463,000,000, is greater than
the whole net income of our farmers in 1938; in other words the cost of production had risen to a larger extent than the entire net income in that year. That struck me as a serious factor in the prices now under discussion, and that is one point I draw to the minister's attention.
When I asked the question about cost of production I was hoping it might be put in tabular form, because I have had to look at the figures on this page to get the information. I believe I am correct in my computation from the minister's own figures. This is a point which struck me as alarming.
It is still alarming.
What was the gross figure?

These figures are given at page 3392 of Hansard, where we find the gross for 1946 is given as $1,759,000,000 and for 1947 as S2,213,900,000. Then we come to the net for 1946 given as $1,267,000,000 and for 1947 of $1,259,000,000.
There is just a small correction. For 1946 the net is $1,160,760,000. Apparently the figure 7 was displaced.
That was the point which struck me as disturbing in connection with the statement the minister made that day, and the argument he was building up today.

Before dealing to some extent with some figures to which my leader the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has just referred I should like to express my appreciation of the comprehensive statement the minister has just placed on the record. While he was doing that, however, I could not help thinking of the old saying I have heard many times in years gone by, that figures do not lie, but that some people can do some terrible things with figures.
It appears on the page of Hansard which my leader quoted that back in 1938 the net income of farmers right across Canada was $387,000,000. From such a statement the word would go out among our people that the farmers of Canada had received a very tidy sum of many hundreds of millions of dollars; yet I am sure the minister will admit that in 1938 thousands of farmers were working long hours to produce foodstuffs at less than the cost of production. The minister covered the period from 1938 to 1947, and for nearly half of that time far too many farmers in this country were producing foodstuffs at less than the cost of production. I think the
Supply-Agriculture

minister, on sober reflection, will realize that the fault lay in the fact that on a previous occasion he had given the people in other parts of Canada the impression that farmers could produce wheat for forty cents per bushel.
Referring to page 3393, I find the minister said this:
We like to talk about irrigation developments; we like to talk about waterpower developments and great expenditures of money. We have got into that habit, but I would not care how- close a power line was to my farm, I would not put electricity on to the farm from a power line.
That statement is also bound to be misleading to many people. The minister went on to say that for a reasonable sum he could have a windmill or wind charger on his place. While I agree that you could have a wind charger in many parts of this country that would supply a certain amount of electricity, the fact is that there is as much difference between that type of power and what you would obtain from a power line as there is between electric lights and the old coal-oil lamp. I know from my own personal experience, and others have had the same experience, that when I had to get along with a wind charger I thought that we were just a little ahead of the coal-oil lamp days. There certainly is no comparison with the benefits to be derived from the use of power from a power line.
I have not the exact quotation before me, but I am given to understand that on a previous occasion the minister said that he did not want a tractor on his place. So far as I am concerned the minister can continue to operate his farm with oxen, and in all probability he would have a good form of farm power. But it would be similar to the agricultural policy of this country. In many ways that policy is still in the oxen days.
We sometimes use a lot of figures to indicate the picture we want to show, but that does not get us away from realities. The fact is that a major industry of this country, even during the boom period brought on by the war, had to wait two or three years or more to get the benefits of the wartime increases. This industry now finds itself with its reserves being depleted, owing to the rising costs of everything that goes into farm production.
I come now to the position of our farmers as far as coarse grains are concerned. I contend that we have been in a muddle from last fall until the present, and in all probability we shall continue to be in a muddle right on through, with the minister and his department and his associates in the government sitting there waiting for something to turn up. The

coarse grains situation will go down in the history of farming in this country as one of the severest letdowns that any government has ever given the farming population.
Our farmers produced coarse grains in spite of drought and other handicaps, and even with the limited number of bushels they were able to produce they continued their deliveries. Yet the people who were in need of coarse grains found that they could not get supplies. Then the minister comes along with a halfthought-out scheme-I almost said "half-baked"-whereby the people who handled coarse grains would compensate the farmer. I shall not go into the details except to point out that this simply created a worse position than we had before.
Under the economy in which the minister apparently believes I contend that he had no right to ask those people to make a refund. While the farmers were entitled to compensation, that was not the fault of these people. Like any businessman they simply took advantage of a situation which the government had handed to them on a platter. If anyone should make compensation, it is the government. Some of the elevator companies continued to let coarse grains go into the ordinary channels of consumption in an orderly way, and they will not have as much to return in proportion to the others who held on. You find yourself in the position where it is hard to justify that action either to the farmers or to the other people involved.
Then there is the other idea of the government making adjustments over and above that. I should like to know when those adjustments are to be made. On different occasions the minister indicated that he was waiting for further word from some of these grain handling firms. It is a plausible explanation, but it does not relieve the situation of the farmers. Will these payments be made some time when it is opportune? If so, just how soon that may be, I do not know.
Has the hon. member had his?
So far as coarse grains are concerned, no.

To whom did you
deliver?

I delivered mine to the pool elevator. Every bushel I produced since we have had a pool elevator in our neighbourhood went to that pool elevator. I have no regrets with regard to any grain I produced that I put through the pool. I also wish to

Supply-Agriculture
say to the minister that I got everyhing I had coming to me for the grain that I delivered to the pool elevator.
You will get your oats and barley payments also.

I will, but the minister uses the most unfair method in trying to make somebody else straighten out the mess that his own department and his government have been responsible for.
This year, as the hon. member for Souris has just said, because of the lateness of the season we shall in all probability have more coarse grain seeded than before; yet we do not know what the government's policy is to be on coarse grains. They say they are waiting. When a certain act was under consideration we were almost daily urged not to delay the proceedings and thus hold up the passage of the measure. What do we find now? There does not seem to be any great hurry at all. They are trying to shift the blame onto the provincial governments, as my colleague said. The government in Saskatchewan acted rapidly. The producers in Saskatchewan are depending on the federal government to do something about the very thing they seemed to be in such a hurry to pass through this house.
I have often complimented the Minister of Agriculture. Perhaps he did not always appreciate the compliments I extended to him, but I do believe that the minister is one of the few members of the government who really has a grasp of the department over which he presides, and that makes me feel all the sadder. Why the minister will so often take only one side of the picture, and a certain set of figures, and then proceed to justify the stand of his department, I do not know. I am prepared to be fair with the minister, but I do not like to be put in the position in which hon. members from agricultural districts find themselves when they try to present the viewpoint of the people whom we represent, and the minister rises in his place, either in the committee stage or in formal debate, and tries-not in so many words, but in the way that he knows best- to confound us. For instance, the other night he referred to wind chargers. Does he think that those of us who have lived out in that country do not know anything about wind chargers? The same is true of the whole list of things that the minister tries to put across. Sometimes I wonder what he has in his mind. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that he had better go out to Saskatchewan and find out what the people there think of him.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that the hon. member for Stanstead is not in his seat. I have the figures which he asked for, and I think I had better put them on the record so that they will be close to the question which was asked.
The question asked was: What proportion of the milk produced is utilized for different purposes in a year? I think it will serve the purpose to use the year 1947, because the proportions are just about the same back to 1931. Therefore I shall put the one year on the record.
The total production of milk in 1947 was
17,213,900,000	pounds. The amount that entered into butter was 8,133,300,000 pounds, or 47 per cent of all the milk produced. The amount that entered into cheese was 1,375,-
900,000	pounds, or about 8 per cent. The amount that entered into concentrated milk was 655,900,000, or 41 per cent. The amount that entered into ice cream was 335,900,000 pounds, or 2j per cent. The amount that entered into fluid milk sales was 3,462,200,000 pounds, or about 21 per cent. The amount that was consumed on farms was 1,722,900,000 pounds, or about 10 per cent. The amount that was fed on farms was 817,200,000 pounds, or about 5 per cent. These figures indicate the ' amount that enters into the production of each product, and I think they will answer the question asked by the hon. member for Stanstead.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the statement just made by the hon. member for Humboldt with regard to what was said the other night. After listening to it I can agree with the first remark he made that figures never lie-"but". The suggestion has been made, and it has been made continuously since 1939 that I made a certain statement in the House of Commons at that time. No one believes that I made that statement except a few members of the C.C.F., and they have continued to peddle that statement ever since 1939. My hon. friend repeats it on the floor of the house now. As a matter of fact, the figures which were used were quoted from the findings of a gentleman, Mr. Hope, who is today one of the leading organizers for my friends of the official opposition. I am quite sure they will believe that any figures he put out at that time were authoritative and correct. The figures were to the effect that it cost a certain amount to seed and harvest grain. My hon. friends have continued ever since to convert that statement into meaning that the Minister of Agriculture said it cost that amount to
Supply-Agriculture

produce grain, which, of course, is an entirely different thing. Again I repeat that while figures do not lie, there is a "but" in them.
The statement which was made a few moments ago with regard to wind chargers is another one which I presume is being prepared for a similar purpose. The only statement I did make the other night on which I have had any comment from Saskatchewan is that one. It may surprise my hon. friends to know that a gentleman who covers the greater part of the province of Saskatchewan in very useful employment wrote me to tell me that he agreed with it one hundred per cent.
He was not selling them?

No; he is selling the gospel, as a matter of fact, and therefore usually tells the truth. He has remained with the job that he started with when he had his first call to the ministry, and therefore, when he makes a statement, he continues to tell what is actually true with regard to the matter.
That would not be the Premier of Saskatchewan, would it?

The fact of the matter is that ever since I have been in western Canada the people have been talking about getting power from the development of water. I left Ontario in 1901 and they were talking then about hydro-electric development in that province. I remember that in the evening around the fireside, the chief topic of discussion on the farm on which I resided, was this very one, and it was said that one of these fine mornings we would have a radial line, propelled by hydro-electric power running down right in front of our house, and we were all going to have electric power on our farms.
Me too.
Me too, my friend says. Well, that was away back in 1901. I own that farm today, and the first power line that came by it came about five years ago.
Mine hasn't come yet.

As soon as the power line did pass it, I put power on that farm and it is there now, so I know something about the cost of hydro-electric power. But returning to the west, I went into the legislature of Saskatchewan in 1914, and I remember one of the first speeches I made in the house. It is still on the record and is still to be found widely quoted in the press of that day. If my hon. friends will take the trouble to look it up they will see that I was advocating the development of hydro-electric power in Saskatchewan.

Some years later, in 1928 I believe, as premier of the province I established the first power commission in Saskatchewan and that gave us government-produced, -distributed and -operated power.
I had long since got by believing that we could cover Saskatchewan in any reasonable time with hydro-electric power. We have verv little of it yet. The power which we have in the province is developed from the utilization of coal and gasoline, and one of their lines runs within two miles of my farm. I could put power on my farm from that line, but it would cost me more to put that power on my farm than it did to put there the plant that I have, and then I would have to pay for the juice after I had got the power there. Under the present plan I do not need to do so.
So far as I know, and I think I know as much about it as anyone in Saskatchewan, there is no possibility of having any considerable water-power development in that province inside ten years.
Except in the spring.

Except in the spring, my friend says. There is no possibility of building the type of dam and putting in the form of construction that is necessary to have hydroelectric power in Saskatchewan on any large scale inside of ten years. I do not know whether I shall be alive ten years from now.
Oh, yes.
My friend has more confidence in that respect than I have.
You will be leader of the official opposition.

Whether I am alive or not, however, I do know that I will not wait ten years to get my house lighted with electricity. As a matter of fact, I gave up waiting fifteen years ago. I think it is very much better to have whatever you can get from a wind charger in the meantime than it is to go without and then stand up in this house, as a member from Saskatchewan, and describe conditions, as my hon. friends of the C.C.F. have been describing them for some time.
Your wind charger is not wearing out anyway.
We have been hearing a great deal of complaining about the amount of wind we have in Saskatchewan, blowing the soil around.
There will be lots in a month's time.

It will be mostly put out by C.C.F.'ers, and I am not so sure it will be

Supply-Agriculture
in a month's time. It may be my friend has inside information which I have not got. There are some reasons for believing that it will not be in a month's time. There is some reason for believing that there were things that happened within the last two weeks in Ottawa which may make it inadvisable for it to be held within the next thirty days. In any case, out in Saskatchewan we did have a considerable movement of wind-
Oh, oh.

-and I am one of
those who believe that you ought to harness what you have got. If the waters do not flow in the right places to permit our developing power, and they have not made it possible for us to develop it for the last forty years, and if they are not going to make it possible to develop power over the next ten years, then I think a good way to provide power is to put up a few wind chargers so that we can have light on our farms. If we find after a short time that it serves as well as the other would, and at less cost, then if we are wise we will keep it. I think it is necessary to say that much in order to avoid having to explain later what was said with regard to the matter.

In view of the statement which the minister has made, considerably clarifying the short statement he made the other night, will he please inform me why his protege in Saskatchewan, the present leader of the Liberal party there, is advocating the electrification of the province in a hurry?

Yes, I will explain that. The hon. gentleman in question, who is not a protege of mine but the product of a very good Liberal convention, and also a product of his own activity in Saskatchewan over a considerable time, will be premier after the election, and when he is premier of Saskatchewan he will make good use of the next ten years in seeing to it that waterpower is developed in the province if at all possible. That policy he has outlined very carefully for the people of Saskatchewan, and he has added to it exactly what I have said, that in the meantime the people have this other means of supplying themselves with electric power on their farms, which they should utilize to the greatest extent possible.
The suggestion has been put forward by the hon. member for Humboldt that some time ago I made a statement in the house, under conditions similar to these, with regard to the use of tractors on farms. Of course, members who were here will know that statement is not a true account of what happened 5849-236
at that time. Six members of the C.C.F. got up, one after another, and said in this house that I knew that it cost less to produce grain with a tractor than it did in any other way; and after six of them had made that statement I got up and made a very short correction, that all I wanted to say about it was that I did not have a tractor on my own farm. My hon. friend can put whatever interpretation on that he likes, but I did not at any time say that it either would or would not pay to have a tractor on my farm. I said I did not have one and I can still say that. I have not one yet. He can take whatever meaning he likes out of that statement, but to get up now and say that I said that farmers could not produce their grain or crops or operate their farms successfully with a tractor or to better advantage with a tractor-well, no such statement was ever made in this house by me, and is not being made in this house by me now.
Then the hon. member made some suggestions with regard to coarse grains and what has happened with regard to them, and what is going to happen. My hon. friend had a lot to say for the Saskatchewan wheat pool. He said he had never delivered any grain to any other organization since that wheat pool was formed, and he never intends to deliver any grain to any other organization so long as that wheat pool exists. This question he has been discussing has been discussed with the Saskatchewan wheat pool on three different occasions. It is the only organization in western Canada that asked the government to wait until May for their final figures with regard to this matter-the only organization. They suggested to me when making that request that I was quite free to mention it on the floor of the house as a reason why we are not making settlement prior to the month of May. I repeat that statement now for the benefit of my hon. friend, in order that he may go back and ask the wheat pool authorities whether that statement was made.
I may say that there are seven companies which have paid. The Premier of Saskatchewan, at a public meeting the other night, in Saskatoon I think, said he was prepared to give the stuffed head of a cabinet minister to anybody who could show him that any payments had been made under this arrangement. I reply to that by saying that seven companies have already made payments to farmers, and very considerable payments, ranging up to 14 cents a bushel, in order to take care of the situation which developed as a result of what was done on the 21st of October last.
Supply-Agriculture

The only reason for this government not taking action before now is the request that was made to us by the Saskatchewan pool that we wait until after the month of May in order that they themselves might be able to act in the manner in which they considered it wise to act.
May I add this, that so far as any information available to me is concerned I have reason to believe that the farmer is not going to get less because they did that. My hon. friend suggested a few moments ago that it would be to the disadvantage of the farmers of western Canada because some companies were waiting until after May and allowing the grain to pass through the ordinary marketing process before determining what they were going to pay out to the farmers. I repeat that the only organization which suggested that we wait until after May was the pool organization, and so far as information available to me is concerned, there is not going to be less paid because they did that, but very likely there will be more. The criticism therefore is one which not only stands against the government itself but stands against the pool, the one organization which did the thing which has just been criticized by the member for Humboldt.
I make this statement at this time only to indicate to my hon. friend that while I have listened to quite a number of statements similar to the one he has just made and have not [DOT]taken the trouble to answer them in the past, now that he has recited at one time all these jokes with regard to agriculture it gives me an opportunity to deal with them all at one time, and if there are any more criticisms of that kind I shall be pleased to deal with them also.

I should like to make a few remarks about the beef cattle and hog industries, and ask the minister a few questions in regard to them. Before doing so I should like to say, in connection with what was said a short time ago about stocks of stored meat, that it would be an excellent idea if the minister would go before the prices committee and explain just what the situation is in regard to stored meat. The last figures available from the bureau of statistics for April 1 showed that our stocks of stored meat at that time were the highest we have ever had in Canada, particularly of pork. I think the figures indicated that there were in storage some 86,000,000 pounds of pork and 36,000,000 pounds of beef. If those stocks have now very considerably declined I think it would be an excellent idea if the minister

would make that clear before the prices committee. It would save a great deal of time and prevent the misapprehension from getting abroad throughout the country that there is an oversupply of meat in storage at the present time.
Dealing now with the hog industry, a considerable portion of the minister's remarks on the last day we discussed this matter, April 27, was devoted to the hog industry, chiefly in an effort, I thought, to produce reasons, other than the policy which he has followed, to explain the tremendous reduction which has taken place in hog production in western Canada. One of the reasons he gave was that the farmers there preferred to grow grain rather than to produce hogs. I thought that was very much on a par with the answer the minister gave me in our discussion last year when he said that a lot of the farmers there were too lazy to raise hogs. I do not think the minister should try to find what I would call piffling reasons to explain the drop in hog production. The minister put some figures of hog production on the record a few moments ago for 1939 and 1947-

Yes, 1946. Those figures did not seem to jibe with figures I have here. It is a table entitled "Hog Gradings by Provinces of Origin", got out by the dominion bureau of statistics. It shows that the production of hogs went up very considerably during the war in western Canada, and went up also, but to a lesser degree, in eastern Canada. Since 1944 hog production in western Canada has been coming down just as rapidly as it went up, and it has now reached approximately what it was in 1939, whereas hog production in eastern Canada has remained up at a high level. The figures are these. Hog production in Alberta in 1939 was, in round figures, 979,000 head; in 1944 it rose to 2,981,000. Production went down a bit, by about 1,000,000 head, in 1945, when the figure was 1,946,000. In 1946 it went down further to 1,250,000 and in 1947, 1,105,000, or to 88-4 per cent of the 1946 figure, and bringing hog production in Alberta down to only 100,000 more than it was in 1939. The same story is true of Saskatchewan. The figures are these:

I should like to understand the effect of those figures. I understood the hon. member to say he was quoting the inspected slaughterings?
No; this table is called "Hog Gradings by Province of Origin", and I understand shows the actual production.
That refers to hogs that are graded at the plants; it is not exactly the production.
It is the production apart from hogs slaughtered in butcher shops and on farms.
The figures I quoted are complete, including local slaughterings as well as the slaughterings in plants.
Those include estimates of local slaughterings.
Those are the figures which come out year after year.
Nevertheless they are estimates.
So are your figures.

I do not think we need quarrel over each other's figures. I think there is no doubt that several circumstances have contributed to this situation. In my opinion the chief cause has been the policies followed by the government in regard to subsidies on feed grain and freight assistance. That has been the chief reason for this terrific reduction in hog production in the west and the increase in hog production in the east. Whether this method of raising hogs in Canada, growing grain in the west and shipping it east to be fed here, is in the best interests of Canada as a whole I think is an arguable proposition. Good arguments might be put up on both sides, and I am not going into that.
Tell us about that.

It may be that it is in the best interests of Canada as a whole. Of one thing I am certain, however, and that is that it has not been in the best interests of western Canada or of western Canadian farmers. I believe that can be readily demonstrated.
Why not?

If my hon. friend will keep quiet for a moment I will explain. It has not been in the best interests of the western Canadian economy as a whole, and of western farmers in particular, first, because it has reduced the income of western farmers. They would have had a greater income and more money would have been available for spending purposes in western Canada if those hogs had been produced there instead of the grain being shipped out. On that point I think there can be no argument.
May I ask a question?
I am quite willing to answer a question.
Do you actually object to the western farmer getting a market in eastern Canada for his coarse grains?
I think I explained at the beginning-
No, you didn't.

If the hon. member had been paying attention he would have followed me when I said I was not arguing whether or not this policy was in the best interests of Canada as a whole, that it was an arguable proposition. I am merely making the point now that as far as western Canada is concerned it has not been to its advantage or in

its best interests, because in the first place it has reduced1 the total income of the western farmers. The second main reason, I think, is that it has reduced the fertility of the land, because of the fact that they have been shipping the grain out of the province.

Might I ask another
question?
Sit down.
I think the hon. member would be willing to answer it.
Sit down.

I think I should be allowed to ask this question. Is it not true that the coarse grains were stacked up on the prairies, that every available space was full of coarse grains?
Why were coarse grains stacked up out there?
And we provided a market for them.
I am quite willing to answer any pertinent questions, but I do not think we are getting any further ahead with this debate by interruptions of this kind.
Well, tell the whole story.

To return to what I was saying, I believe the second important reason why this policy of growing the grain in western Canada and shipping it east to be fed to hogs and cattle is not in the best interests of western Canada is that it is reducing-
Why not give us a chance?

-the fertility of our soil. If the hogs were fed out there, everything produced on the farm would go into the hogs and return to the soil, and you would not have anything like the loss of fertility that occurs when you have to ship out the grain. For these two reasons, the smaller financial return to the farmers and the loss in fertility, I believe there is no question that this policy is bad for western Canada and for the western Canadian farmer.

However, Mr. Chairman, to a large extent that is history, and I should like now to turn to what might be called the immediate and future questions in the minds of the hog producers, which I should like the minister to answer. The evidence before the prices committee during the past two or three weeks has been that at the end of the year we shall probably have a surplus of pork after we have filled the United Kingdom contract and supplied the domestic market. I should like to ask the minister, first, what he proposes to do about this surplus if it develops? I hope he will not get up and say there will be no surplus, because, as I say, the best evidence we have been able to get so far is that in all likelihood there will be.
That there is a surplus.

After I have resumed my seat, which will be in a minute or two, I should like the minister to tell us what he proposes to do with this surplus if it develops. Then I should like to know if there is any possibility of increasing our shipments of pork to the United Kingdom beyond the amount called for under the contract. My third question is whether the new contract the minister will be negotiating shortly will be for an increased poundage.
In that connection I should like the minister to say something also as to the probable prices under the new contract. A short time ago, in placing his figures on record, he said that in 1946, under the bacon contract, the price was $22.50 up to April 1 and $25 from then to the end of the year, and that the price under the 1949 contract with Great Britain would not be less than the average of those figures. I should say that average would be about $24. The minister knows as well as I do that it is no comfort whatever to the hog producers of this country to learn that the price under the bacon contract for 1949 will be not less than $24. The present price is $36. Everyone who knows anything about the hog business knows that a price only two-thirds as high as the present price would put practically all the producers out of business, that it would break anyone depending on the production of hogs for his livelihood or a major portion of it.
Could the minister give some better assurance than that to the committee and the country, and particularly to the hog producers, as to what the prospects are for 1949? The questions I have been asking are very much in the minds of hog producers. They are entitled to know what the situation is likely to be next year, so that they may be able to make their production plans accordingly. They

Supply-Agriculture
have to start in on that shortly, and at this time they should know where they are likely to get off.
I would ask the minister to comment on one further point. Apparently the effort of the government at the present time is to bring down the price of pork-to bring down the prices of everything and thus to reduce the cost of living. We have had a great deal of discussion on this matter in the prices committee. There seems to be no question that the evidence presented is to the effect that the only way in which the price of pork to the consumer can be brought down materially at the present time is by reducing the price to the producer.
This idea of bringing down prices has been put out by the minister's colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when he states that these prices must come down. This is disquieting to the pork producers and farmers generally. The producer feels that a threat is hanging over his head, to have his prices forced down in order to appease the demands of consumers for cheaper bacon and cheaper pork products generally.
In reply, would the minister give some reassurance to the pork producers in this matter? I think the minister and all hon. members realize that it is most disquieting to find the papers filled almost every day with talk about the possibility of the government's imposing controls on this, that or the other thing to bring down prices, and that prices are to be forced down by it. The producer is left in the position where he thinks: Well, I am going to be the goat, as usual.
He never is the goat.

I suggest that the minister should give some reassurance to hog producers on that point. I have a number of questions I should like to ask about beef, but I shall take my seat in the hope that the minister will answer my questions concerning pork.

I think the hon. member began his observations about meat, generally, including beef, and completed his remarks by a more specific reference to pork. The same could be said concerning the discussions in the prices committee.
I talked about nothing but pork, with the exception of my reference to beef in storage.
In the last five minutes.
Everything else was with regard to pork.

The points raised by the hon. member for Souris had to do with beef prices and the sending of beef to the United States. Then, within the last five minutes the matter has been largely with respect to pork supplies. Perhaps it would be just as well if I were to refer to both of -them when I am replying, discussing one immediately after the other.
I turn first to the questions asked by the hon. member for Souris in connection with beef, and beef shipments to -the United States. I do not think I need go over the history of the matter.
Excuse me-
Now, if my hon. friend will let me answer-
I had quite a number of questions.
And the hon. member will receive answers to all of them when he comes to them-if hon. members will allow him to ask them.
My way might save time.
When I am answering these questions I should begin by answering those asked first.
All right.

The suggestion was made some time ago that we ought to send our beef to the United States. This, of course, would have had the effect of greatly increasing the price of beef at least in this country. Cattle have gone down about ten cents a pound since then.
What?
About ten cents a pound in the United States.
Oh.

And of course there
is not nearly the same urgency, apparently, for a discussion of the question at the present time. When it was being discussed on a previous occasion I made the suggestion that probably the time would come much sooner than hon. members expected when floor prices established by contracts would be worthwhile.
The other day Mr. Ross, who has been one of the chief critics from Alberta, a man who is an outstanding rancher, and whose opinion is always valued on the question-
That is George Ross.

Yes, George Ross. He is reported to have said to the committee
Supply-Agriculture

that grass cattle shipped from Montana comparable with those shipped from Alberta would bring on the United States market $22 and on the Canadian market $16, for a comparable grade. That is a difference of only six cents a pound. When one considers that there is duty to be paid-and it is not high-and that there is freight to be paid, he can conclude that the margin between American and Canadian prices is not nearly so wide as it was when we were discussing this matter in January. In other words, roughly speaking, the price of cattle on the United States market has gone down about ten cents.
For the benefit of hon. members in the committee, may I say it is not possible any longer either for them or for me to suggest that this is a question which is under the Department of Finance. It has been transferred back to Agriculture.
Entirely?
So I can now discuss it as the minister who may have something to do directly with what is to be done from now on in regard to the export of beef.
Is it entirely under agriculture now?

I shall explain the whole position. Hon. members should know, from legislation we have passed within the last few years concerning these matters, that we did set up an export organization in the Department of Trade and Commerce. It has always been the situation throughout the years that the Department of Trade and Commerce has handled the actual export of products. Where it is necessary to have permits, that department issues those permits. But permits are and always have been issued on most agricultural products under the advice of the Department of Agriculture, or at least on the recommendation of that department.
In 1942 the authority to make that recommendation in connection with beef cattle was transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the prices board in order to give that board full control over prices in Canada. Now -today-it has been transferred back to the Department of Agriculture. So from now on, recommendations made in the matter will be made in a greater degree as related to the actual conditions surrounding the necessity for marketing.
I wanted to say that to the committee, in order that we might be clear as to the exact position at the present time. However, that has been the position for only a few hours; therefore we are all starting off with the same knowledge. I may say there are two or three

matters which have to be discussed when the question is being considered, with reference particularly as to when and how any product may be returned to the United States market when it has been out of that market for some time. In connection with beef, however, there are special conditions. One has to do with the fact that the quota, prior to the war, for entrance into the United States, from all the world, was 220,GOO head at a weight of 700 pounds or more.
We had an agreement with the Americans that our proportion of the quota was to be about 76 per cent, and that the Mexican quota was to be about 24 per cent. When it was determined that our beef was to go to Britain under mutual aid, while United States cattle, beef or pork, or anything of that kind, was going to Britain under lend lease, we were asked to release the United States from the obligation to keep the Mexican supplies down to 24 per cent and to let them take whatever proportion of the total amount of 220,000 head or more that they desired to take. Naturally that was agreed to. We were given the undertaking at the time that, when the position was reversed and we were again shipping cattle into the United States, the fact that we had not done so in the meantime would not have any bearing upon any decisions that might be reached but that the question would be considered on its merits at the time.
We have come back to the time when some consideration will be given to the matter. In answer to the question asked, I cannot say when cattle will be shipped to the United States, but I can say we are going to open up negotiations as to what will happen when cattle are shipped to the United States. Of course the situation has changed somewhat. The cattle producers represented to us and we represented to Geneva that, because we had shipped about 525,000 head of cattle in cans and frozen, and otherwise, to Great Britain and Europe in 1945, we were likely to have considerably more than the 193,000 head which was our part of the 220,000 head quota under the old arrangement when the war was over and when we had settled down to produce.
Because the producers felt that way, and the government agreed, we made representations, and out of the discussions came the fact that there is no change in the duty on cattle under the Geneva agreements. The president has the right to reduce duties by 50 per cent as he had back in 1936 and 1939. In 1936 and 1939 we got the duty of $3 per hundred cut in two, making it $1.50. Under the present arrangement the president may cut the duty again by 50 per cent in connection with the Geneva agreements which were on the basis

Supply-Agriculture
of the same quota, but out of the discussions came the fact that the quota was to be 400.000 head and the duty to remain as it was. The duty has not been changed.
We are confronted with the situation where all the world has a quota into the United States of 400,000 head of cattle, but there are only two places from which they can get any considerable part of that quota. One place is Mexico and the other is Canada. We must negotiate what proportion of that quota we are to have. One of the facts with which we shall be confronted is that last year we did not have 100,000 head to send out of Canada and it does not appear that we shall have any more this year. This is largely because we are consuming 25 to 30 per cent more beef in Canada this year than we were in the years before the war.
These questions still have to be discussed with the United States before the United States boundary line is opened. All I can say is that they will be discussed and at an early day. Questions have been asked witl. regard to shipments to Great Britain. Storage., at April 1 of both beef and bacon were very high. So far as cattle are concerned, this was due to something which, so far as I have read, has not yet been brought out before the prices committee.
In December last year we had quite a long discussion about the removal of controls on meat ceilings and coarse grains ceilings and out of that discussion came certain ideas. One was that there would not be nearly as many hogs marketed in 1948 as had been marketed previously. Another was that we might have more beef marketed than had been marketed in some of the earlier years. It was anticipated that this beef would be marketed at *the usual time in considerable quantities, namely, around the end of March or the beginning of April.
Farmers in eastern parts of Canada have been accustomed to filling their stables with feeder cattle in the fall and feeding them with grain, either produced by themselves or purchased in western Canada, through until the latter part of March or the early part of April. That provided the full winter program on many farms in the eastern part of Canada. In the month of January we found that beef cattle were coming on to the markets, particularly in eastern Canada, in numbers away above what was expected. We made enquiries with regard to it.
I sat in on discussions with men who buy cattle in areas in western Ontario where cattle are produced and from which areas they were coming onto the market in great numbers. I was told what obviously would be true. In December we decided that, since
there had been an increase in the price of grain through the ceilings having been taken off, there ought to be an increase in the floor prices under livestock in the British agreements. This house was assured that those contracts were being negotiated and eventually would be announced and that they would be satisfactory, provided that prices of feed grain remained at rates which were considered to be reasonable when the increases were added.
At the time we were discussing the matter, barley was selling at around $1.20, and oats at a comparable figure. We said in this house that was a reasonable figure in relation to the price of wheat and therefore it was a reasonable figure upon which to estimate or work out prices that ought to go into the British agreements on all farm products produced from feed grains.
Unfortunately barley went up to $1.36 a bushel in January; it did not stay at $1.20. Obviously farmers who were feeding hogs could not act as did those who were feeding cattle. Farmers who were feeding cattle fed some Ontario soft wheat and to that extent they did not feed barley. By the middle of February we had a large percentage of these cattle in cold storage in our packing plants. Those cattle had been bought at about one cent a pound below what the market had been at the beginning.
Instead of having the cattle standing in the stalls and feeding down to the end of March, we had the beef in cold storage in the plants. There was so much of it that we had to ask the British to permit us to send part of their second quarter's supply over in advance to be stored there. On the other hand, feed grain accumulated. We did not have sufficient storage space in which to store the beef. It is some of this beef which appears in the storage figures around the end of April, and some of it still appears in the storage figures in May. But as to any suggestion that it was some manipulation on the part of somebody or other that brought about the situation, particularly if that somebody or other is someone who was handling beef and buying cattle, I think one has to go farther back in order to have the full information that is necessary to come to a proper conclusion with regard to the matter. Also one has to know that much of this beef which was in storage was beef that should not have come on the market at all until the month of April. Had it come on the market in the month of April, there would probably be 100 pounds more on each steer; we would have had beef to send to Britain in greater quantities than we did; we would probably have on our own market more beef of the type which people
Supply-Agriculture

want to buy, and prices of meat might not have gone up as high as they did in April.
I suggest that there is m that some explanation for what has happened in connection with beef. But the present position is that we have practically no beef in storage on this side of the Atlantic at the present time. We have not been buying beef since early in the month of April to fill the British contracts. We have been leaving the beef cun this market in order to assist in providing that beef would not go up to higher levels than it went during that period of time. It is true that there is a shortage at the moment. Part of the shortage is due to the facts which I have indicated, and part of it is due to the fact that they could not deliver cattle in western Canada during the month of April. Floods and road conditions have been such that cattle could not be brought in. That has had some effect upon the number of cattle that are coming on the market, and therefore the amount of beef which is available, and may have some effect upon the price which is being paid.
The storage figures for the month of May are not in my hands at the moment. I have heard approximately what they are, but I do not want to guess. I shall put them on the record later if I have them while we are considering these estimates. Of course they are much lower than the figures were at the first of April. Much that beef has been consumed. There is involved in that the other question as to when we are to open the United States marke'.
Coming to bacon and hogs, we were told, as I suggested a moment ago, that our production of hogs in this year would not be as high as it was last year. I must admit that the suggestions which were made in the house and outside the house, in newspapers right across the country, did, I think, mislead some of those who were making statistics with regard to what the situation would be. At the time that the discussions were taking place, we in the department increased the figures by 20.000,000 pounds above what we were told, by the best statisticians that we could consult, would be the amount of bacon which would be available in Canada in 1948. Even those 20,000.000 pounds do not take care of the amount of bacon that is coming in, or the number of bacon hogs coming in. We received 48 per cent more hogs on the market in January than we received in January the year before, and we continue to get hogs in greater numbers than were estimated prior to the beginning of the year; with the result, as was suggested a

few moments ago, that more is coming on the market than the British contract, as drawn up. will take.
Mr. BURTON . Will the minhter permit a question?

Let me finish my statement. In direct answer to the question as to whether Britain will take more, up to the present time Britain has taken more. I am not going to try to guess what she will do in the future, but up to the present time Britain has taken more than the contract calls for. Our weekly shipments have been 25 per cent over what the contract calls for. If we were to continue at that rate the total amount of 195.000.000 pounds would be delivered by about the middle of September. Because of that, I am not in a position to say whether we shall have a surplus of hogs in 1948 or not.
During the years when we were on the upgrade, I was accustomed to taking chances in stating figures to the house, and I must say that I never over-stated them. After adding from fifty million to seventy-five million pounds to the figures which were quoted to us as the amounts that farmers would likely produce in bacon and ham, we have found that every year during the war the farmer exceeded those figures, and went on up into other figures until late in the war. More recently, when the production is on the downgrade it is just a little more difficult, because in the earlier period we were trying to coax the farmers up to higher levels.
My hon. friend has asked me, what about the future? I do not know that there is anyone in the world who can say very much about the future at the moment. All I can say is that there is not anyone who is asking us at the present time to send hogs to the United States, because the Canadian market is the highest market in the world that we can find for Canadian hogs. Hogs are selling in Canada at a higher price than they can be sold anywhere else. The United States market is lower than ours. So far as we know, there are very few places where pork can be sold at the price at which it is being sold at the present time in Canada. I state that because it is a fact. I do not say where this is going to take us, but I do say it is an indication that farmers did require floors under their prices in 1948 in the form of British agreements. It is an indication that the government was not short-sighted when it had these contracts drawn, and established the position that the farmer could be sure of, up to certain dates. Beyond that, I am not prepared to go at the moment.

Is the minister prepared to say anything as to what plans are being made, if any, to deal with this surplus if it develops? I think the minister said it was probable that there would be a surplus.

That depends. There will not be a surplus if the British continue to take it in quantities sufficient to take care of it. We figure that around the middle of September, as they have been taking it, we would come to the point where the figures would turn the other way for a time. Whether they do or not depends upon the attitude of the farmer himself. If he thinks the returns are so good that he is going to increase, we may be wrong in our guess that the quantities will come down somewhat from September on to the end of the year, comparable with the deliveries of a year ago. I would not care to say that. I am certain at this moment that we shall have more than we can handle under the British contract, but I suggest that the British are taking more than the contract calls for at the moment, and may or may not continue to do that right through the year.
What we are doing in relation to the surplus now is finding the best markets that we can find for hog products. Small quantities have been sold in Europe. Perhaps additional quantities can be sold there. This will be all sold under arrangements which will be satisfactory in relation to prices we have under the British contract. I am not in a position to say more than that with regard to production or with regard to marketing. The situation is as I have described it.
What about the new contract, as far as increased poundage is concerned?

That will be discussed on the basis of the facts as they are at the end of the year. The discussions with the British with respect to the new contract have usually taken place in November and December, as was the case last year; no doubt they will take place at the same time this year, and the decisions reached will be based on conditions then existing.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to rise to a question of privilege. I may say that I have no desire at any time to put a wrong interpretation on any statement made by any member in the house, and as I mentioned at the time I was speaking a short while ago, I did not have Hansard before me with reference to the statement to which I referred. The Minister of Agriculture having made his statement following my short remarks, I should like, as a matter of privilege, to put on the record now what appears in Hansard of April 5, 1939, on page 2623, in the first column, where the right hon. gentleman makes this statement:
It has been proven over and again that twenty bushels to the acre of wheat can be produced at a cost of from 30 to 40 cents a bushel. We have had a great deal of discussion about the cost of producing wheat. It costs a certain amount to work an acre of land whether you get any wheat off it or not; it costs a certain amount to harvest it if you do get any wheat off it. It has been proven over and over again, I say, that twenty bushels to the acre of wheat can be produced at a cost of from 30 to 40 cents a bushel. For every bushel a man gets over twenty his costs per bushel decrease. When he has a crop of twenty bushels or more per acre, his other crops are usually good in proportion.

There were some more interjections and then the minister said:
You will find upon a close study that he arrives at pretty much the same figure I have given.
At no time, however, did the Minister of Agriculture state that he was quoting from Professor Hope's finding, and if I erred in making the statement I did I apologize to the minister. Certainly I had taken it in good faith throughout the years as the record appeared.
The statement which my hon. friend has read is never read in that form to an audience in Saskatchewan. If it were I would not take exception.
I have never quoted it any other way.

The statement made in Saskatchewan is exactly as the hon. member gave it this afternoon, that I had said that the cost of producing wheat in western Canada was the figure he used. When he reads the article, it is clearly indicated that it is the cost of putting wheat in the ground and taking off the crop, and I even go so far as to state that if you add debt costs and other costs you get a higher figure. When I was asked where

the figures were quoted from I said Saskatchewan University, and Mr. Hope was the man who was compiling the figures in Saskatchewan University. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) then used those figures to indicate that when you take another set of figures and add them, namely, the full cost of the production of wheat, which is interest on the money invested in the farm, returns to labour for farmers and all those on the farm, and all that kind of thing, you can get a higher figure than that. But that is the actual cost figure for seeding an acre of land and harvesting an acre of land. That is made obvious by the fact that the discussion which was then on was a discussion as to whether it made any difference whether the land was light or heavy, and I think I used arguments at the time to indicate that there was a difference.

I find no place here where the minister referred to Professor Hope as the authority for the figures he had given until there were interjections, and then he said that Professor Hope arrived at approximately the same figure he gave.
The university record is Mr. Hope's record. There was no one making records but Mr. Hope.

Will the minister answer the last question I asked in regard to the apprehension which hog producers feel at the present time over the statements made by some members of the government with regard to pushing down pork prices, among others? I asked that he might make some statement on that which would serve as a reassurance to those people who are becoming increasingly nervous over constant reports in the papers as to what might be done by way of controls and otherwise to effect that purpose.

I have not heard the remarks made by any minister and therefore I am not going to comment on them. I have seen headings in the papers to the effect that certain things were said before a committee, but my memory was that it had to do with meat prices, not pork prices particularly.
I think the minister will admit that the price paid for hogs determines largely the price that people have to pay for pork.
Beef is included in meat.

The producer is interested in the price he will get for his hogs. I know the minister reads the papers regularly, and he has seen, as I have, dozens of these

reports. I wish he would say something which might serve as a reassurance to the hog producers and put their minds at rest.

It is evident from certain action the government has taken that there are surpluses of certain meat products in Canada. They opened up the market in the United States for certain types of canned beef, pork and other meat products. At least some of the farmers are alarmed that the government opened that market to the packers before opening it up to the beef producers. I put a question on the order paper some time ago as to quantities that were being exported. They were not large quantities but in the total it is rather a considerable amount. To the question I put on the order paper regarding the quantity of canned beef, pork, or other meat products at present allowed to be exported to the United States, the following answer was given:
X. (a) Spreads and potted meats, 579,000 lbs.; (b) pork products, 207,000 lbs.; (c) solid pack, other than pork products, 283,000 lbs.; (d) stews, boiled dinners, hashes and chile con carne, 833,000 lbs.
The total is 1,952,000 pounds, for which permits have been granted or are in process of being granted. When we export our coarse grains we export them under a permit system whereby any money that is made on the export of those grains comes back to the producers, but apparently the United States market has been opened up to some extent to the packers without any guarantee that any additional revenue obtained from that market will come back to the producers. Can the minister say to what extent this market is being opened up and why it should be done in this way?
It will be noted that the figures are about 1,000,000 pounds.
It is 1,950,000 pounds.

The total kill of beef alone in a week is about 10,000,000 pounds, and when you take even 2,000,000 pounds it is a small part of what is being consumed in Canada. That, of course, is not the answer to the question which has been raised. The price of livestock would be somewhat lower- it might be only a small fraction of a cent-if it were not possible to get rid of the trimmings. These trimmings may be partly fats and partly other meat, but they are all mixed into a product called pressed meat, or they may be canned into a product called canned meat. To say that they cannot have a market for them when we are shipping the quantities of bacon, ham and beef we are shipping to Britain, and

Supply-Agriculture
when there is no market for the trimmings in Canada, would not be helping anyone. As to the suggestion that a great profit is made on the trimmings, I am not so sure about that.
I did not say there was a profit.

I doubt if there would be sufficient involved in it to make any great difference to the farmers who are delivering from two to three hundred million pounds of bacon and some hundreds of millions of pounds of beef. What is done with these trimmings in cans would not make much difference to the farmer. If you tried to distribute it, the costs of distribution would eat it up, I should think.

Is it the policy of the government to open the United States market to the packers ahead of the farmers in shipping beef over there? This is an indication that the United States market is being opened to a certain extent.

I do not know just what process we shall go through to have the market completely opened, but when it is opened, cattle will be marketed just as they were before the war, so far as the machinery for marketing them is concerned, but I hope they will not be marketed at as low a return.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to change the subject for a few minutes, and I do so only because I have to go away. I want to ask the minister about another matter about which I wrote him and wrote the Minister of Finance and wrote the governor of the Bank of Canada, last summer.
I found that we had coming out to our part of the country quite a number of men from the United Kingdom, men who were very well off. I remember one in particular whose ancestors had a great deal to do with producing some of the types of cattle which are now so popular. I mean cattlemen from generation to generation. What they were anxious to do was to buy a place in this country and operate it, but they had, of course, no means of getting their English money out here for that purpose.
The question I asked Mr. Towers and also the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture was roughly this. Here were these men ready and willing to give, not only security on the places which they had at home in Britain, and they were large substantial places, but also security on the places in Canada which they wished to purchase for the purpose of continuing to breed prize livestock,
the best of breeds and the best of cattle. It struck me, not being a financier, that we could not possibly lose anything by that.
Obviously the Bank of Canada must have credits in the old country. The reply I got from Mr. Towers was that he could not see very much wrong with it but that it was a matter of government policy and therefore he could not give me an answer. The Minister of Agriculture was away at the time. I did receive a reply from someone in his office but I never had my question answered. I do not say that in any blameworthy way. I realize how busy the minister was, and I am grateful for the courtesy that I got from his office. I wonder if he would tell me if that could not be worked out.
One can readily see what a splendid thing it would be for the whole livestock industry in this country if we could get these men, experienced as they are, not only in raising livestock but in improving the breeds, established out here. Some of them are credited publicly with improving the breeds of cattle. I think it was they who eliminated the daylight between the animal's belly and the ground; in other words, they started getting the beef down close to the animal's heels.
I cannot see very much wrong with this scheme, nor can I find any reason-it may be that I am just ignorant; I do not know-why there should be any exchange problem at all. We take security over there, and ample security; we take another security here, and all we do is to provide them with the dollars necessary to build up those ranches in this country. I am referring particularly to some people from Scotland. Perhaps the minister did not get my letter. I wonder if he could enlighten me, because surely it would be a splendid thing for our cattle industry if we could have investments of that kind made in the Dominion of Canada.

I am no more, probably not as much, a financier as the hon. member for Calgary West. I do not know if he was at a gathering the other nighb-I think not- at which Sir Albert Braithwaite spoke. I mention him only because the same question was involved in connection with coal mining. The question raised has been discussed many times, and I have no comment to make on the answer my hon. friend received from Mr. Towers. After all, government policy on matters of this kind must be determined to some extent on the advice the government gei3, and there are men who have made a thorough study of the question and who do give advice.

Sir Albert was very critical much along the same line as that taken 'by the hon. member for Calgary West, as to why such a thing cannot be done. He said he had these very large holdings in Britain which had been taken over by the British government, and he had the British government's paper that so much money was coming to him; but when he went to the Bank of England to try to get dollars to bring to Canada, and put his security behind that request for dollars, the Bank of England told him he just could not get the dollars. Apparently this is a matter where considerable negotiating would have to be done, not only with the British but with the Americans and some other people.
