Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: The minister's statement that hog deliveries were on the increase was surprising to us from the west. May I ask what per cent of these slaughterings was due to deliveries of breeding stock?
Just about the normal percentage of breeding stock. The figures I have given and the fact that pork is in storage for Great Britain indicate that these were mostly A and B hogs.

Much of the information the minister has given to us this afternoon underlines the contention of the members of this group, namely, that you cannot have a properly balanced agricultural economy when you have fluctuating prices. The minister gave earlier the production in Canada in 1946 as compared with the production in 1939; but in doing so, as he said, he was taking a year after the war and comparing it with a year before the war. I would say he was taking a period when there had been little planning, and comparing it with a period which followed a time during which there had been a good

deal of planning, and when many of the benefits of that planning were still being felt. I believe farmers generally feel that during the last part of the war at least, they were doing fairly well. They considered their economic position much better than it had been for a long time. They do not want to go back to the situation that existed before the war; they do not want the conditions which prevailed then to prevail again; but every step the government has taken since the end of the war has been in the direction of the same kind of economy that we had before the war, and we are seeing the results of that policy on every hand.
The minister gave figures showing increased marketings of pork earlier this year. I do not know what is happening all across Canada, but I know the people in my area are getting out of hog production. They had a number of hogs last fall. They did not want to exterminate them, so they decided to fed them; and as quickly as possible they are getting those hogs on the market and getting out of production. The minister says he does not know what the deliveries are likely to be this fall. I believe deliveries would be much better if the farmer had a reasonable idea in advance of the amount he will earn if he feeds hogs. The minister said the marketings of cattle were increased in the first part of this year because the price of barley was very high. That definitely supports the contention of this group that the high price for barley was not benefiting either the farmer who grew it or the man who had to buy it to feed to his livestock. That price was benefiting only the middleman, and was imposing a hardship both on the man who produced the grain and the man who bought it for feed.
The discussion this afternoon has been interesting and entertaining. I do not think the debate on windmills and wind chargers was serious. I do not believe the minister really thinks a wind charger can provide all the power a farmer could use on his farm if he were getting his electricity at a price similar to that which, for instance, the people of this province have to pay. However, I believe the farmers of Canada and in particular those of the western provinces will solve their electricity problem, provided that they have a decent income each year. Give the farmers of western Canada a decent income; let Saskatchewan continue to expand its power development at the rapid rate it has shown in the past few years, and to sell that power at the lowest prices in the history of that

province, and the people of Saskatchewan will solve their electricity problem to their own satisfaction.
I would not wish to say, as one hon. member suggested, that the hon. member for Rosthern is a protege of the Minister of Agriculture. If he is, I think the hon. member has gone far astray. As I understand the minister's ideas, he believes in undiluted Liberalism, but the hon. member for Rosthern is getting a lot of non-Liberals around him. I doubt that he will ever be premier of Saskatchewan. The minister said he would; then five minutes later went on to say, "You know, I am not one to prophesy what is going to happen in future." If the hon. member for Rosthern ever should become premier, however, I do not think he will head a Liberal administration. He may think, "Well, now, I have a few members here elected on the Liberal ticket, but by gosh I think they are Tories," because down in my part of the country the strategy of the Liberal party is to go out and nominate as the Liberal candidate a well known Conservative, and then try to have him accepted by the members of the Liberal party.
In the constituency of Bengough rumour has it-I am not saying this is true, but I have heard it so often I think there must be some foundation for it-that a well known Liberal, with whom I am sure the minister is well acquainted, and who was a member of the legislature at one time, wishes to run as an independent Liberal. That is the only way he can support Liberalism in that constituency, because he does not like the Tory candidate the Liberal party has nominated to contest the seat. So I say the hon. member for Rosthern is not really a protege of the Minister of Agriculture, because he is doing many things I am sure the minister would not condone.
In his remarks the other evening, the minister accused members of this party of always saying that agriculture is going down and dowrn instead of going up and up, as the minister said it was. I want to admit right now that during the war the government implemented policies which did benefit agriculture a great deal in comparison with the terrible situation that prevailed before the war. I am quite ready to give anyone, including the minister, who had anything to do with those policies, full credit. But while that is so, the people of this country should not have to be plunged into war before the farmers are given a decent standard of living. Farmers say what wre did during the war we can do during the peace, and we can do it even better because we have more people in Canada who can produce the things we need.
The net position of agriculture in 1946 was somewhat better than in 1947, but even so I do not believe the position of agriculture in 1946 was as good as it should have been. In that year the net income for all Canada was something over $9,600 million, while the net income of agriculture was $1,267 million. In other words, twenty-five per cent of the population, which is approximately the percentage employed in agriculture, received much less than twenty-five per cent of the national income. A twenty-five per cent share of the national income in that year would have amounted to approximately 82,400 million, while agriculture actually received only half that amount. So that, while in 1946 agriculture was in a relatively good position compared with other years, certainly it should have been in an even better position.
To come to 1947, according to the minister's figures the gross income of agriculture improved by some $455,000,000. Farmers' gross income improved by $455,000,000 and their net income dropped by $8,000,000. I suggest that those figures condemn the policy which the government has followed in the last two years, the policy of taking off all controls and all the protection farmers had, and turning them back once again to the vicious and gambling grain exchange, placing them back once again at the mercy of the machine companies and the oil companies, and what have you. Because of that policy, while gross agricultural income increased by $455,000,000, the net position of farmers, was $8,000,000 worse in 1947 than in 1946.
That deterioration in the position of agriculture was not brought about by crop failures, because statistics show that prices worsened, so far as farmers were concerned. In 1946 the average wholesale index was about 109; in 1947 the average was about 129, or an increase of 20 points. The general wholesale index takes into account all commodities. So that the cost of all commodities in Canada increased between those two years by approximately 20 points. The average index for all agricultural products in 1946 was approximately 112, while in 1947 it was 120. So that prices of agricultural products between those two years increased by only eight points, whereas prices of all commodities increased by 20 points.

I have not been able to follow all the way through the argument put forward either by the leader of the C.C.F. or the hon. member for Wood Mountain. There is, however, a fact which must be apparent to anyone. The net income, after making allowances for all costs, to farmers right across Canada in 1947 was $1,259,000,000. To go back to 1939, to which year the leader of the C.C.F. referred, the net return was $484,000,000. The simple fact is that, after considering all costs, the net returns to farmers are almost three times as high in 1947 as they were in 1939. That is the only point I wanted to make, and what I have said is clear from the figures. The net return received by the farmer over and above his costs was about three times as high.
I admit that the amount way back in 1939 did not even pay the cost of production, which means that the $1,259,000,000 is not an increase in net return in the sense that all the return is net profit. Nevertheless the farmer is getting in return three times as much as he got before.

How does the minister account for the change between the 1946 and 1947
incomes?
I believe there is an error in the figure appearing in Hansard for 1946. I have not checked it, but I am told that the Hansard figure is $1,267,000,000, whereas it should be $1,167,000,000.

I should like to make a few comments on some of the statements made a little while ago concerning the removal of the export ban on beef cattle going to the United States. The minister said that, since the price dropped in the cattle markets of the United States, there had been a great reduction in the amount of talk with respect to the removal of the ban. So far as the beef men in my province are concerned, I am not aware of any reduction in their talk on the matter, or any lessening in their demand for the removal of the export ban. Those men have been asking for the removal of the ban, not chiefly from the point of view of price, as the minister knows, but from that of ensuring that the United States market for Canadian beef will be kept open, as they have expressed it, and retained for the future.
I do not think there has been any change in that regard, so far as they are concerned. The minister said that when Mr. George Ross appeared before the prices committee he indicated there would not be a great deal of difference between present prices received by United States ranchers across the border in Montana and those received by Alberta ranchers along the border. The minister gave a fairly accurate report of what Mr. Ross said, when he pointed out that there was a difference of about six cents a pound.
If I might be permitted to correct the hon. member-and I know he is not attempting to misrepresent what I said-
No.
I did not say that; I did not make the statement the hon. member attributed to me. I gave the actual figures; and later on I did say freight and duty had to be deducted.
I was making the suggestion that they would have to be shipped to Chicago; the freight rate from Winnipeg to Chicago would have to be added.

We can pretty well leave out freight. It might amount to a little, but not very much. The duty is H cents a pound, so that there would be a difference of from 4 to 4J cents a pound. I thought the minister left the impression that that did not amount to anything, and that, therefore, as far as prices were concerned, the beef-cattle men were doing quite well and did not need to worry about that 4\ cents a pound. I do not think that is the situation at all.
If I left that impression it was not intentional.
That is the way it sounded.

Yes, that is the way it sounded; and I should like to make it clear that that 4 to 4} cents a pound is important to the beef men. As a matter of fact, if it had not been for the rise in beef prices during the last three weeks a large number of feeders in western Canada would have lost a great deal of money. How they will come out now, I do not know, but they certainly needed the rise that took place in order to have a chance of getting out.
The minister indicated that he now has control, more or less, of agriculture, particularly as far as the export of cattle is concerned, back in his own hands. I understand that this took place within the last day or two. I am glad to hear that, because I would hope that now there will be a much better chance of getting action in opening up the United States cattle market. I trust that the minister will, in the near future, exercise the powers which have been returned to him.
He stated that there was a quota of 400,000 head to be allowed in at a duty of one cent and a half and that it would take some considerable time to negotiate with the United States as to what proportion of that quota we could have, provided that any cattle could be shipped. He said at the same time that the only other source of supply was Mexico. I think the minister is well aware that no cattle are allowed into the United States from Mexico because of the foot and mouth disease which is prevalent in that country, and the probability is that none will be allowed in for several years to come. I cannot see why any negotiations with the United States government are required as to how that quota of 400,000 head is to be split up between ourselves and Mexico. I do not think there is any question but that we could have all of it at the present time.
We have no chance of filling it at the present time, although we might have if we were sure that it would be there for the next two or three years.
I can see no real difficulty in having this export ban, as far as the United States is concerned, removed immediately. I think the only reason the United States would not be opened up is that which has been given by the minister throughout the country on several occasions, namely, that the ban was being maintained in order to prevent domestic prices of meat from going up. Of course that is a different question altogether.
I have in my hand a letter written by Mr. Charles H. McKinnon, president of the Western Stock Growers' Association, who lives near Dalemead, a few miles east of Calgary. This letter is addressed to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King under date of March 27, 1948. I should like to ask the permission of the committee to have this letter placed on Hansard, because I think it presents the views of the western cattle producers in as clear and complete a manner as I have ever seen them presented.

Yesterday the leader of the house refused a similar request by the hon. member for Lethbridge, and I note that there has been some favourable comment on the action which was taken. Simply to have a letter, written by someone and not read in the house, placed on the record is objectionable.

If there is objection I shall have to read it. I thought I could save a little time. After I have read it, I hope the minister will make some comment on the questions, both direct and implied, contained in the letter. The letter reads:
March 27, 1948.
Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I have been instructed by the board of directors of this association to write directly to you in connection with Canada's beef cattle industry. The decision for this instruction was arrived at only after full discussion of the industry and government policy during the war and the post-war period.
Supply-A gricullure

The beef cattle industry is one of the important basic industries of Canada. In western Canada it is basically of greatest importance because cattle population related to human population reveals that Canada's surplus cattle marketings each year are produced in the west. If you will examine the record you will find that the industry since its inception in the early eighties in western Canada, despite wide variations in climatic conditions, has always managed to carry itself without assistance from the federal treasury. It has done this primarily because of the fortitude of its operators, their willingness to take bad years with the good, managing to carry cash and feed reserves from good years to bad.
As you know, and for which the industry gives you full credit, the Canadian-United States trade agreement in 1936 marked a new era for the industry. Access was then possible to the great United States market for a quota number of cattle at a reduced rate of duty. Until 1942 our operators had a close, quick and profitable market for their surplus production. With the exigencies of the war and the establishment of the wartime prices and trade board finally came the embargo on Canadian exports. This was accepted by the industry as a war measure and it was understood that the right of export of live cattle would be lodged with the food corporation which was organized as a crown company by the prices board. The main purpose of the corporation was in times of sur plus to purchase live cattle at Canadian ceiling price equivalents, export the same to the United States in order to keep trade channels open and if a profit should accrue to keep the same for the future benefit of the industry. Despite the appearance of surplus marketings, and the decline of live cattle prices below dressed beef ceiling equivalents with embargoes placed in some instances on public markets, the corporation failed to discharge its main purpose and beef cattle producers were obliged to absorb the shock of price decline. Despite representations repeatedly made to your Minister _ of Agriculture and your chairman of the prices board, nothing was done. Our surplus production was purchased by the meat board and sent overseas to feed our troops and those of the United Kingdom.
With the commencement of mutual aid and lend-lease, we made no further representations when we were assured that our outlet to our natural United States market would be protected for the post-war period. We were disquieted when the chairman of the meat board ventured to state that the United Kingdom market would be substituted for the United States market, and were further disturbed to learn that our surplus production was diverted to Europe exclusively and wras not available for the Alaskan theatre of operations where Canadian troops were stationed. Instead, supplies were drawn from as far south as Omaha, Nebraska, and Kansas City, Kansas. We were in a position from Edmonton via Prince Rupert to aid the war effort and at the same time this action would have assisted in maintaining live cattle prices close to the beef ceiling equivalent.
During the war period, producers were concerned chiefly with preserving friendly contacts and their natural outlet to the United1 States market.

I should like to emphasize that sentence particularly in view of wnat was said here this afternoon by the minister and myself. I continue:
They had given up the American price in the interest of inflation control; their chief concern was that of preserving the market to the south and suggested on different occasions that token shipments should go forward. This was in accordance with government policy as stated by your Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with other Canadian industry. W1' were also concerned about your Minister of Agriculture's flat beef ceiling policy and its effect upon the feeding phase of our industry and made representations for upward revision of the ceiling during the first half of each year By acceding to these requests the prices board was able to keep cattle feeding on an even keel.
When the war concluded in Europe and with Japan, the industry naturally looked forward to decontrol and to the restoration of the right to private export of cattle. The operators were soon to be disillusioned, however. Despite the At1 antic charter declarations to which our gov ernment heartily agreed, and despite the possibility of favourable entry into the United States for Canadian cattle under international trade talks (subsequently confirmed by announcement of the terms of the Geneva trade agreement which is operative since January 1, 1948) your Minister of Agriculture again despite opposition of the industry's national beef council, proceeded to the United Kingdom and egotiated beef contracts with that nation. 1 officials of the British food ministry had stated that the United Kingdom could not be expected to be a purchaser of Canadian beef during the post-war period. The low-cost countries such as Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil would be the chief suppliers to that market.
In comment on this I may say, Mr. Chairman, that one of the things our cattlemen have found most difficult to understand is this. We have never had an explanation why the United Kingdom was forced to enter this beef contract at a price much higher than they were prepared to pay or at which they could get the supplies from elsewhere, and at the same time the beef men were cut off from the higher price market in the United States.
That statement is not correct, Mr. Chairman.

Well, I have read the letter and I am just making that comment on it. I shall continue with the letter:
Let us for a moment analyse the present position of our beef cattle industry.
Price controls have been removed on practically everything beef producers purchase for use in their operations, yet the ceiling of prices written into a new United Kingdom contract continues. Price ceilings on the domestic market had been removed and prices commenced to rise to reflect increased feeding costs. Instead of your government undertaking to explain the seasonal rise, propaganda against

Supply-Agriculture
the rising price of beef was, if not condoned, unanswered, and instead a threat of a reimposition of price ceilings overhangs our market.
That is the very point, Mr. Chairman, that I asked the minister to make some comment on, and to give some reassurance to the pork producers this afternoon. Apparently he was unwilling to do that. I should like to know if the beef cattle producers are in the same position. They have a feeling of apprehension because of this threat of ceilings being imposed and their prices being forced down In a large number of cases that would mean serious losses, if not bankruptcy for some of them. I go on with the letter:
The ceilings on barley and oats which are the main coarse grains used in cattle feeding were removed at the commencement of the 1947 feeding season and immediately prices went to a higher level, approximate]} 80 Der cent higher than previously obtained. At that time a packing house strike of employees gripped the nation and it was stated that meat ceilings would be lifted after the conclusion of the strike. This was done, but in a surplus-producing industry we soon found that the United Kingdom contract price was a practical ceiling for our production. As a result today our feed lot operators are faced with heavy losses on their teeding operations.
We also respectfully call your attention to the fact that during the war and afterwards, other phases of the cattle industry have not been accorded such inconsiderate treatment. Dairy cattle producers have had no restriction placed on their exports of live cattle to the United States. In 1947 they exported 53,474 head and in 1946, 68,995 head which compares to less than 15,000 head prior to the war. The producers of registered purebred beef-type cattle have without interruption been able to export their surplus production to the United States during and since the war and they have realized full American prices. We have just witnessed the spectacle of ithe Canadian rancher sitting beside an American rancher at the Calgary bull sale. For the bull the American rancher would have to pay the equivalent of three two-year-old steers; the Canadian rancher, assuming he didn't drop out of the bidding, would have to offer the equivalent of five two-year-old steers. Is it right and fair that the commercial cattleman should be subjected to such unfair competition? Our men, who by and large are considered fair in their appraisal of business relationships, cannot understand government allowance of this discrimination.
Foot and mouth disease in Mexican herds has resulted in a United States embargo on shipments from that country. Nearly 500,000 head of Mexican cattle were previously exported each year to the United States market. With Mexico now eliminated, and in the opinion of your own veterinary director general and many others qualified to express an opinion, for many years to come. Canadian beef cattle producers have an enlarged opportunity for profitable export. The Geneva trade agreement provides for 400,000 head annually of cattle weighing 700 pounds and over to be admitted to the U.S. at 1J cents per pound duty and an unlimited number over that figure at 2J cents per pound duty. For the first time, the industry, from a marketing viewpoint, has a potential which it has not had since the years of the first world war when cattle were admitted to the U.S. without limit and free of duty. Our men cannot understand your Minister of Agriculture's appraisal of our future markets when he insists upon binding our industry to the unnatural United Kingdom market with contracts against which cattlemen have unequivoeably taken their stand.
We hear repeatedly of U.S. dollar shortages and we cannot understand why one of Canada's basic industries capable of earning from $60 to $80 millions of U.S. dollars annually by exporting to its natural market is denied by the action of the government of Canada access to it. Instead is substituted an austerity program and excise taxes which increase the cost of living and in the case of cattle producers who must purchase many taxed items for their operations, increasing production costs.
We receive letters from your prices board pointing out that the average price of beef cattle the first part of this year was higher than last year. In this way they attempt to placate our cattle feeders. They do not have anything to say about the higher cost of feeder cattle last fall and the 80 per cent rise in the price of coarse grains. We learn that Canadian packers are allowed to export to the U.S. (and to receive the U.S. price) fancy meats such as tongue, hearts, livers, etc. We learn that they have never been restricted on their exports of beef to Bermuda or controlled on the price they receive for those exports.
Mr. Prime Minister, it is the duty of this association, which has represented the cattle industry in western Canada since 1896 to outline this unpleasant state of affairs in our industry and to request that you take an active and personal interest in the same.
Your Minister of Agriculture, at our 52nd annual meeting held at Lethbridge on January 15 portrayed himself as supporting the United Kingdom contract without reservation. He attempted to lead those present to believe that the United Kingdom negotiators did not haggle -"did not spend 10 minutes in his office". He said nothing about a subsequent meeting to be arranged prior to March 31 with UK. negotiators to discuss ways and means of payment. His officials knew within a million pounds or so what surplus the beef cattle industry could produce in a given year. He estimated our surplus for 1948 would be 45 million pounds. "If we had thought we could sell more we would have written in more". Yet already over 60 per cent of the 45 million contract figure has been purchased by the meat board for export to the United Kingdom and the year is not one-quarter finished and our heavy fall marketing period is ahead of us.
At this livestock convention and after giving your minister a fair and full hearing, the heavily attended session voted unanimously the following resolution: "That this meeting go on record as favouring the restoration of the right of private export of cattle and to all the benefits accruing therefrom."
It may be of interest for you to note that your Minister of Agriculture at Woodstock, Ontario, on February 22. when addressing the Oxford county federation of agriculture, is reported by the press to have said, "I still believe
Private Bills

that the United States' market is the natural outlet for Canadian beef cattle and this country-must get back into it as soon as we can." This was only five weeks after the Lethbridge appearance of your minister, yet he completely reversed himself. Small wonder our men are greatly confused.
At our recent directors' meeting, it was voted unanimously that we take our stand in unalterable opposition to the state marketing of our products under contracts. "We are a free country of free men and we favour free enterprise, a system which has been responsible for the growth of this nation. We are opposed to state socialism, to communism and we will not desist in our battle for the restoration of the right of private export."
Mr. Prime Minister, in all of the years in which I have actively engaged in cattle ranching, over 30 years, I have never seen such an unrest among our people. There is a feeling of frustration: a denial to them of what they know to be inherently and basically right. This matter of restoring the right of private export and the cattle industry to its rightful owners is a serious business. We implore you to give your personal attention to this matter. A continuation of present policy can only in our opinion undermine the confidence of the people in established authority and result in a permanent dislocation within Canada's beef cattle industry.
We would deeply appreciate a reply to this letter. My apology for its length, but it could not have been shorter. A copy is being sent to each of your ministers-agriculture, finance, and trade and commerce-and in due course it will be given widespread publicity.
Respectfully yours,
Chas. H. McKinnon.
President.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house in committee on Bill No. 151, to incorporate the National Insurance Company -Mr. Rinfret-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall section 1 carry?

I rise to record my objection to the adoption of section 1 of this bill. There are, Mr. Chairman, quite a number of insurance companies underwriting life and fire, as well as general insurance, which are concerned about the adoption of this section, and have raised strong opposition to it, for the obvious reason that to grant such a name as the National Insurance Company to this company would create con-

fusion in the minds of insurance purchasers as to the exact identity of this company. Referring to the list of insurance companies registered to do business in Canada under the Canadian Insurance Act, 1932, as extracted from the Canada Gazette of April 10, 1948, I find ten different insurance companies using the word "national." We have the National-Ben Franklin Fire Insurance Company, the National Fire Insurance Company, the Nationale Fire Insurance Company of Paris, France, the National Liberty Insurance Company, the National Life Assurance Company, the National-Liverpool Insurance Company, the National Provincial Insurance Company, the National Retailers Mutual Insurance Company, the National Surety Corporation and the National Union Fire Insurance Company. The representatives of a company whose original name was "The Nationale Fire Insurance of Paris, France," ask us to grant them a new incorporation of their parent company in Canada under the name "National Insurance" which, in my opinion, comes in conflict with the name of many outstanding Canadian insurance companies, and which will lead insurance buyers in Canada to confusion, and might cause prejudice to insurance companies which, through years and years of steady work, sacrifices and sound management, have succeeded in building up prestige for themselves, and have identified their success with the word "national" in their organization.
No objection would be raised if the sponsors of this 'bill would consent to add something to the name of the company they wish to incorporate which would identify the company more specifically, as for instance, "National Indemnity Insurance Company," or "National Casualty Insurance Company." But no; in spite of all suggestions made to them, in spite of representations made in the banking and commerce committee by the attorneys of two outstanding insurance companies, the National Life Assurance Company of Canada and the National Fire Insurance Company of Hartford, no compromise has been reached so far in order to meet, to a certain extent at least, the suggestions made by these companies concerned.
May I point out that, because of my close association with the National Life Assurance Company of Canada, I refrained from voting in the banking and commerce committee on this matter. Furthermore, and for the same reason, I shall also refrain from voting in the committee of the whole should there be a division on this question.

Private Bills
We welcome foreign capital, but not at the expense of the prestige built up by our good, secure and soundly administered Canadian insurance companies and the British and American insurance companies doing business in Canada.
We understand that this company seeks incorporation because of the fact that its parent company in France has been nationalized by the French government. Therefore this new company's intention is to take over the Canadian interests and assets of the Nationale Fire Insurance Company of Paris, France. Why should not they continue to do business in Canada under their original name, since they have used that very same name in Canada since 1914, I understand? Furthermore, I consider it my duty to warn my hon. colleagues of all parties in the house that to grant such a controversial name to this company, without giving more careful consideration to this matter, might lead to serious implications in so far as the rights of the provinces are concerned in matters of insurance.
According to the provisions of the British North America Act, and many decisions of the judicial committee of the privy council, insurance is a subject which has been declared of provincial competence, although it is true that the federal government may incorporate companies with federal objects. I shall quote a few of the decisiona of the judicial committee of the privy council. In the cases of Citizens Insurance Company v. Parsons, (1881) 7 Appeal Cases, 96, and John Deere Plow and Wharton v. the King, (1915), Appeal Cases, 330, the judgments declared that a province cannot pass an act which comes in conflict with the functioning of a company which was granted a federal charter. Here is another decision of the privy council: Great West Saddlery v. the King, (1921) 2 Appeal Cases, 91. The same principle applies in this judgment. The judgment reads:
The provinces cannot sanction an act which would paralyze the functioning of a federal company, but the general laws of the provinces are applicable to federal companies as for instance, imposing taxes and laws respecting mortmain.
Another judgment is that of Bonanza Creek Gold Mining Company v. the King, (1915) 50 Supreme Court Reports, 534, which states specifically:
The provinces have the right to incorporate companies wit-h power to be exercised within the province and also to give a general power similar to the power of a physical person which might be exercised all over Canada.
The last quotation is from a judgment of the judicial committee of the privy council, in re The Insurance Act of Canada, (1932) Appeal Cases, 41, which states specifically that:
A foreign company-
And that description can be applied to this particular case.
-having obtained permission by virtue of provincial law to do business in a province is not under obligation to obtain a federal permit.
Any federal legislation imposing the necessity of a federal permit .in this case would be unconstitutional. Furthermore, the federal authority cannot intervene in the business of insurance, since this subject is declared to be exclusively of provincial competence.
There are three ways by which a company may incorporate to sell life insurance or general insurance in Canada: through the request of the Secretary of State, through an act of parliament, or by virtue of an act of the provincial legislature. Therefore, to adopt clause 1 of this bill, without seeking the official opinion as to whether or not this name, the National Insurance Company, does come in conflict with the use of names of insurance companies incorporated in the provinces, is a greater responsibility than I wish to take as a member of this house.
I know of at least three insurance companies incorporated by the legislature of the province of Quebec which bear the word "national" in their name. In order to seek that information which is not yet available to this committee of the house, I communicated with the undersecretary of state, in the following terms:
Ottawa, Ont.,
May 6, 1948.
Mr. AY. P. J. O'Meara, K.C., .
Asst. Under-Secretary of State,
West block,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. O'Meara:
As you are aware, there is now before the House of Commons a bill which has passed the Senate, entitled: "an act to incorporate the National Insurance Company". This bill is bill 05 of the Senate. The name to be given to the company, is. quote. "The National Insurance Company" and in French, "La Nationale Compa'gnie d'Assuranee".
My purpose in writing to you is to obtain from your department an official expression of opinion as to whether the names suggested would not come in conflict with names of existing companies, whether federal or provincial.
In other words, I would like to know, if, for instance, a similar application was made to the companies' branch of your department, it would be decided if whether or not, in view of the existence of similar companies (federal or provincial), the above mentioned names could be granted.
It is true that parliament is supreme and can decide to allow the incorporation under the names suggested, on the other hand, neither the Senate nor the House of Commons is in a position to know whether there is conflict in the names suggested without the advice of the government officials who have made a life-long practice of deciding the suitability of names suggested in cases of companies incorporations.
Private Bills

The difficulty resides, as far as parliament is concerned, in avoiding the use of names of companies incorporated in the provinces, or of names in conflict with that of any provincial company. It is evident that the duty of parliament in Ottawa is to protect, at all times, existing provincial rights, and it would no doubt be an invasion of those rights, if we were to give to a federal company a name already existing in any of the provinces or a name in conflict with any similar name in existence therein.
I would be grateful to you, as the matter is rather urgent, if I could have an answer at your earliest convenience.
I remain, dear Mr. O'Meara,
Yours very truly,
I wish now to table a copy of this letter and move that clause 1 of this bill stand until the officials of the Department of the Secretary of State have furnished this committee of the house with their official opinion as to whether the name "national" does or does not conflict with other names of existing insurance companies doing business under federal or provincial charter.

The name of the proposed company was submitted a long time ago to the superintendent of insurance in Ottawa. He has before him the list of all insurance companies and he himself appeared before the committee when this bill was called there.
The former superintendent.

I was going to say that. Mr. Warwick, the present superintendent being unable to appear before the committee, asked Mr. Finlayson to take his place. Mr. Finlayson has had at least thirty years' experience in this work, and he stated to the committee that in his opinion the name which would be the most distinctive of all under the circumstances would be the name as incorporated in the bill, to wit: the National Insurance Company.
As the hon. member for Bonaventure has said, there are quite a number of other companies with the name "national". There is one he has forgotten and that is the National General, which was accepted and passed by this parliament at the beginning of this year. There is one thing he has not told us either, and that is, which company in particular he refers to when he objects to the use of this name.
If he is referring to the National Life Assurance Company, first of all the name of that company is "Assurance", whereas the name that we are seeking here is "National Insurance". There is quite a difference there, because the National Life Assurance covers all insurance purchasers who want life

insurance, whereas in our case the National Insurance carries all kinds of insurance except life.
The question was put to Mr. Finlayson whether this company, with the present charter, could go into life insurance, and the answer Mr. Finlayson gave was, "No, they cannot. If they wish to have the power to carry on business as life insurers they will have to come back to parliament with another bill and ask for permission to do so". They have no intention of going into that line.
As to the suggestion made by the hon. member that the addition of another name to the word "national" might help, a suggestion was put forward before the committee that this company should take the name of National General. That carried until I brought before the committee the bill which we passed at the beginning of this session.
If we take the name "indemnity" we shall clash with all other companies appearing in this insurance list to which the hon. member has referred, having names in which the name "indemnity" appears. There are quite a number of those.
If we use the word "casualty" we come into conflict with all the casualty companies, of which there are quite a number. That question was also discussed by Mr. Finlayson before the committee; and he said that, since this company has two names, if the name were translated into French it would give rise to serious difficulties and confusion with other existing companies, because if we carried the name "National Indemnity Company", the name in French would be "l'indemnite nationale; " therefore we would cease completely to have the name "national", and the company would be called by the name "i'indcmnite". If we called it the National Casualty, in French it would be La Casualite Nationale, and therefore the name would appear as La Casualite and that would do away completely with the name.
This company has been operating in Canada since 1914. The name of the company, which is mentioned in paragraph 9 of the bill, I believe, is La Nationale Compagnie d'Assurance. That is the name under which the company has been known. In English it was translated as The Nationale Fire Insurance Company of Paris, but the real name of the company is La Nationale, and whenever anybody wants to do business with that company in Montreal they always call it La Nationale. It has been known as that ever since 1914. The word "fire" was dropped in order that the name of the company would not clash with that of the National Fire

Private Bills
Insurance Company of Hartford. So, instead of creating confusion, we are avoiding confusion by adopting this new name.
The hon. member for Bonaventure has referred to foreign capital. This is not a foreign capital company. It is being incorporated with four gentlemen, everyone of whom I know. The capital is all subscribed here in Canada; it is all Canadian money that will go into the company. It is true that it is the intention of the company to buy the Canadian assets and obligations of the French company, La Rationale; but, as I have said, the capital to go into the company will be all Canadian.
The suggestion has been made that we should give a little more consideration to the names of various provincial companies. It is evident from the proceedings in the committee that no company outside of the two that appeared has any objection to the name "National Insurance Company". The two companies that appeared before the committee were the National Fire Insurance Company of Hartford and the National Life Assurance Company. These two companies offered suggestions, and both of them were represented by counsel. Mr. Finlayson was asked to give his opinion to the committee as to the advisability of adopting this name; and he advised the committee that in his estimation, after thirty years' experience as superintendent of insurance, the most distinctive name that could be chosen in the face of the objections of the National Life Assurance Company and the National Fire Insurance Company was the one we have chosen, the National Insurance Company. That distinguishes it from either the National Fire or the National Life.
The hon. member for Bonaventure has referred to various cases that went to the privy council. I know those cases well, and I cannot see how they support his contention. The conflict between a province and a federal company has nothing to do with a possible conflict between a provincial company as against a federal company. Therefore I cannot see why those references were made.
There are three authorities, the Secretary of State, an act of parliament, and an act of the provincial legislature, by which a charter can be granted to an insurance company. That is quite true. It seems to me that the place to make objections was before the committee. If the National Life Assurance Company wanted to make objections they should have appeared before the committee and have come prepared with any objections emanating from the office of the Secretary of State, but they did not do that. They were duly represented before the
committee and made their objections. A vote was taken in the committee, and the result was thirteen yeas in favour of the name National Insurance Company, and six nays against it. After that vote, the name was adopted.
The report mentions that the Hon. Philippe Brais represented the National Insurance Company, Mr. Wilson McLean, the National Life Assurance Company and Jean Martineau, the National Fire Insurance Company. They all had an opportunity to make their objections before the committee.
Reference has also been made to the list of insurance companies. It is curious to go through it and see how many of these companies have similar names. There is, for instance, the Aetna Insurance Company and the Aetna Life Insurance Company. Many companies have the word "American" in their name. There are the American Insurance Company, the American Automobile Insurance Company, the American Equitable Assurance Company.
Similarly "Continental"; is used by four different companies. There is the Continental Assurance Company, the Continental Casualty Company, the Continental Insurance Company, and the Continental Life Insurance Company. It is noticeable that the Continental Life Insurance Company was the first one to be licensed in Canada; it was licensed in 1899. Then in 1910 the Continental Insurance Company made application and got their licence, even though a company already existed known as Continental Life Insurance Company. In 1917 the Continental Assurance Company made application and got a licence, although at that time there existed the Continental Life Insurance Company and the Continental Insurance Company.
Similarly with the word "Fidelity". There is the Fidelity Insurance Company and the Fidelity Life Assurance Company.
Similarly there is the General Insurance Company, the General Accident Assurance Company, the General Accident Fire and Life, the General Security Insurance Company, and so on.
There is the Guardian Assurance Company, the Guardian Insurance Company and the Guardian Life Insurance Company. One of these companies had to exist before the other; notwithstanding that, when the second licence was applied for, it was granted.
The same thing applies in the case of the Home Insurance Company. Another company was afterwards incorporated known as the Home Fire and Marine Insurance Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I may ask a question just for information, in the case of companies such as Western Life Assurance and Western Assurance, do they represent substantially the same interests?

and when there is a third company usually it is Canadian; but they do not represent the same interests. That is why I did not refer to the Prudential company.
In the face of all this, Mr. Chairman, and particularly in the face of the opinion or advice given by the superintendent of insurance, Mr. Finlayson, who has had at least thirty years of experience in these matters, I do not see how we can refuse to accept that advice as well as the affirmative two to one vote in committee. On the other hand, if the hon. member for Bonaventure insists that this clause should stand and the committee favours having it stand until next week, until a reply is received to the letter to Mr. O'Meara, I cannot but bow to that decision, though I doubt whether anything new will come to light.

I intend to support the motion of the hon. member for Bonaventure, because I think the arguments he advanced were sound. I am not a bit concerned about what the insurance companies think, but I am concerned about what the people think; and this multiplicity of names is very confusing to the people. Over and over again I have heard complaint made by people who have been buying life insurance, fire insurance and insurance of other kinds, particularly by people who are not acquainted with the exact name of these various companies. I have known men to make mistakes. I have known of agents soliciting life insurance, and of men doing business with another company which they thought was the same one. I believe the arguments advanced by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat were most unsound. The main basis of his argument was that because we have done things in a certain way in the past, therefore that way must be correct and followed for all time.
This question has been given a good deal of consideration in British Columbia, where they are more careful in such matters now than they were a few years ago. Today the records are searched very carefully to see that a company seeking incorporation does not have a name similar to that of a company already incorporated. I know of a company which sought incorporation less than two months ago under the name Columbia Lumber Company. Because there was another company known as the Columbia Timber Company, the application was refused. Then a company sought incorporation under the name of the Arrow Company; but because there was already a company known as the Arrow Sales Company, that application was refused, on the ground that it would cause confusion in the public mind. Those matters are scrutinized

very carefully in British Columbia, and the reason is that in the past they have found people confused because of the laxity shown then in authorizing similar names for incorporated companies.
Before resuming my seat, I repeat that the arguments of the hon. member for Bona-venture struck me as being sound. I should like to ask the Minister of Justice a question, though I am not quite sure whether he is the proper minister to answer it. Does the superintendent of insurance or any official of this government check with the provincial governments before granting the use of a name applied for by a group who wish to become incorporated?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, it is a bit irregular for a question to be directed to a member who is not in any way connected with the bill, but my recollection is that the superintendent of insurance was always consulted as to whether any confusion would likely result when the name of a new company was proposed. The argument of the sponsor of the bill clearly indicates that already there are a great number of companies in the insurance field with somewhat similar names, and that already there is a state of confusion. Why should that state of confusion be added to by parliament's granting the name "national" to another company which wishes to adopt that name, without any qualification, exclusively to itself, and which name is embodied in part of the titles of many companies already existing.
I believe the argument of the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska is not one which

It may be known in the French-speaking part of the country as the "nationale"; but certainly it is not known, so far as I know, nor does it transact business east of the province of Quebec. If it does, it will run into conflict with the National Life Assurance Company.

arguments of speeches to which I have listened. Whether it was addressed to the Prime Minister or to me-as a matter of fact, I have a copy of it-that is what it is to all intents and purposes, and it would be entirely improper to have had it put on the record of this house without being read to the members so that they could hear it at first hand. As a matter of fact, there are so many statements in it that are not in accordance with the facts at all that it ought to be answered, and answered immediately.
In the first place, the suggestion is made that I went to Britain to get the British to enter into a contract for beef when the British had no desire to have the beef. The facts are that the British at that time were prepared to pay the United States price for our beef to be shipped to Britain and the only reason for not having done so was the fact that their desire did not correspond with our own ideas in this country at that time with regard to price control. They were anxious to get all the beef they could from Canada, and there is no information available to anyone which would offset that fact.
A further fact is that the gentleman who signed the letter and all those who had anything to do with writing it, were sitting at a table in Lethbridge. I think my hon. friend the member for Lethbridge was in the room at the time, when I was asked the question whether I considered that the United States market was the proper market for our Canadian cattle, and when I answered directly that the United States market was the market which would be supplied in the future by our cattle from this country. There has never been any question about that, and when the writer of the letter states that I had reversed my position between the Lethbridge meeting and the Woodstock meeting, he is stating something that is entirely incorrect. The same statement was made at both meetings, and not only that but it has been made at every session of this house since 1942, namely, that the market which would best provide for our surplus cattle' in the future would be the United States market.
The reason the government has not permitted our cattle to enter the United States market up to the present has to do with price control, and not with the question of marketing considered by itself. But, as I have stated today, the position of the government has changed within the last day or two because we believe that the changed conditions both in the United-States market and in this market make it possible to approach the question from another point of view, and that point of view exactly the one which is suggested in the letter should

be followed, namely, that the United States market is the natural market for Canadian cattle.
There are a number of other matters dealt with in the letter upon which I am going to touch as soon as possible, just to indicate that the letter itself is not based upon facts, and not being based upon facts there is very little reason for anyone giving any further consideration to it.
In a number of important points Mr. McKinnon's statements are not in accordance with the facts as established by actual records in Ottawa.
In paragraph 3, on page 1, of Mr. McKinnon's letter this statement is made:
The main purpose of the (food) corporation was in times of surplus to purchase live cattle at Canadian ceiling price equivalents, export the same to the United States in order to keep trade channels open and, if a profit should accrue, to keep the same for the future benefit of the industry.
This statement is, of course, directly contrary to the operating policy announced and followed by the food corporation while it was buying and selling cattle in the year 1942. The operating policy of the company was to buy cattle in Canada at the equivalent of United States values and to sell the cattle to the Canadian meat trade at the equivalent of Canadian ceiling prices for beef. In pursuing this policy, an effort was made to pay to the Canadian producer the equivalent of United States prices for his cattle up to the numbers that might have been shipped under the quota while, at the same time, keeping down meat prices to Canadian consumers. The corporation actually made a deficit of more than $800,000 which, of course, was in line with the policy which the corporation was directed to follow.
It is true that in carrying through this policy the corporation did export a few cattle, but this was done mainly to test the accuracy of the judgment of those who were appraising cattle for the corporation. The financial results
of the exports were that the corporation broke almost exactly even, thus indicating that the appraisers had done a reasonably sound job in estimating the value of the cattle at the time the purchases were made.

Before the minister goes on, may I point out that the sentence immediately preceding where he started, says, "It was understood" by the cattlemen that that was the purpose of this corporation and so forth. Who gave them to understand I do not know.
They had no reason to understand that, because there was an announcement in every paper in Canada to the effect of what I have just given to the committee.
It is only fair to have it appear on the record that they understood that.

What is the date of the letter?

I believe it was dated some time in April; at any rate it was before the end of the first period. The facts are that the beef contract is for 50,000,000 pounds, and that at April 1 approximately 15,000,000 pounds had been delivered on the contract, which is about thirty per cent instead of sixty per cent of the contract, as indicated by Mr. McKinnon. There are other inaccuracies in the letter, but this will serve to indicate the degree to which the letter departs from strict statements of fact.
The memorandum goes on to say:
In the matter of policy, of course, Mr. McKinnon is entitled to hold and to express whatever views he wishes with regard to export controls, price controls and floor prices. However, it may be worth while observing that Mr. McKinnon deals with the beef and beef cattle situation as if cattle alone of all farm products had been subject to export controls and price ceilings. The fact is that practically all farm products were directly or indirectly under price ceilings and export controls during the war. Furthermore, many of the export controls have been continued down to the present moment. The basic reason for this Whole policy was, of course, to retain in Canada sufficient supplies of food to meet the needs of Canadian consumers and to enable the whole price control program to operate. Mr. McKinnon's reference to free exports of dairy cattle and purebred livestock generally has little bearing on the general situation because they do not ordinarily form part of the food supply, therefore free exports had little or no adverse effect on that supply.
In the matter of prices and general economic position, it is a simple statement of fact to say that there has been no consecutive period of similar length when the Canadian cattle industry has prospered to the degree that it has since 1940. This prosperity has been due in part to favourable climatic conditions and in part to rising prices and ready sales for all cattle produced. Early in the war cattle prices rose faster and farther than prices of most other farm products. In the later years cattle prices have been more stable, but they have still tended to rise. Prices for the first three months of 1948 have been higher than for any other three consecutive months since accurate records have been kept.

I must say I was surprised to see the Minister of Agriculture reading a very long typewritten reply to this letter and the remarks I made on it. He and his officials must have been very busy since we rose at six o'clock in order to have this all typed out and ready. It is unlike the minister to read statements; he is one man who stands up and gives a reply more or less right off the bat, and usually in exceptional form. If I had three hours more, probably I could dig up sufficient statistics and figures to throw as much doubt on the figures the minister has just given as he has been throwing on the figures given by Mr. McKinnon, but until I have time to do that I shall say no more on the matter.

Just to conclude the discussion, I may say that I had this prepared in order to answer the letter at the time I received it. After I read the letter, however, I realized that I had answered it all at Lethbridge and other places, and that the gentleman who wrote it had been sitting alongside me, so that I did not think it was worth while going all over it again. I still have the document, and I have given it to the committee this evening in reply to the letter which has been read.

I have a few remarks I
intended to make on the various items as we came to them, but I think everything will be pretty well said before we reach the items. When you have to follow a number of western members who have been speaking on agriculture, and you are able to dig up something new to say, you are going some. Two or three times since this debate started I should have liked to take part in it. I should like to have said something about the windmill business and the use of electrical appliances on the farm, but I am not going to take up time with that; everything has been pretty well said. The only point is that in Manitoba our difficulty has always been to get enough wind to blow the charger. They do not seem to have that trouble in Saskatchewan.
There are not enough members of the C.C.F. in Manitoba.

speechtext: They have a coalition government there; they neutralize each other.

I have had some experience in these things. I am happy to say that this year the hydro came past my farm home, and the dream we have had for many years-I do not know how far back other hon. members go, but we have been talking about it for twenty-five years-has come true. At last we shall
Supply-Agriculture

be able to have these electrical appliances on the farm. Just in passing, may I say that even if hydro had been available before the war I am doubtful whether in some districts of Manitoba we would have been able to sign up enough people to make it worth while to bring it in, but that is not the case today.
I have listened to the arguments about cattle going to the United States. I have always maintained that the United States was the logical market for our surplus cattle. However, we were at war, and we had commitments to Britain. Now, however, I am delighted to hear the minister say that he is going to run this business himself. I do not agree with him half the time or perhaps seventy-five per cent of the time, but I think he will make a better job of it than the Minister of Finance because, while the Minister of Agriculture may have been born in the east he is a westerner now, and he will have to listen to the cry of the west. There are heavy rumblings out there today, and it would be a great help if we could have even a small quota to start with. The hon. member for Calgary East mentioned the situation in Mexico, where the cattle have foot and mouth disease and, as a result, are not allowed to enter the United States. If we could supply those 220,000 cattle it would be a wonderful thing. I think the Canadian Federation of Agriculture sum it up pretty well in their report, in this way:
Having in mind that the United States market in the past has been the only satisfactory long-term market for our surplus beef production, the restoration of this market at the earliest possible moment consistent with the national interest, was strongly urged. Pending this, our delegates again urged the immediate establishment of token shipments as a means of preserving contact with that market.
I believe our ambition should be to get back into that market, beginning in a small way and gradually building it up.
But there is another market I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, in regard to feeder steers. When I was in Britain last I went into this question thoroughly, and there is a good market there for our good-class feeder steers that are not properly finished in the fall and cannot be finished here because they go into the packing plants. They could go to Britain, where they would bring a good price; and we could use the Hudson Bay [DOT]railway to take them out. I think this is Worthy of consideration. I know the price *would be right, and the British farmer wants them for feeding purposes. I might say that [DOT]our steers make remarkable gains over there when they are put on that good feed they have.
A little bit of heather?
Do you feed them oatmeal over there?

I would also call the minister's attention to the matter of condemnation insurance. We have been paying the same rate of condemnation insurance since 1906, and the government has spent large sums in the eradication, of tuberculosis from among our cattle. I suggest that the rate should now be reduced. If the department has been making the progress I think it has, then a rate of half of one per cent is too large. A tremendous number of hogs have gone through; yet there is practically no tuberculosis among hogs. There have been instances where some, trace has been found in their necks, but it has not been much. The disease among hogs has not been serious; yet we have been paying this condemnation insurance on these animals right along. I would ask the minister to do some investigating into the matter. It is something that is entirely in the hands of the packing companies. As the minister has told me before, no one needs to sell his cattle to a packer unless he wants to. But that is our outlet today; there is more stuff going to the packer than ever before. Tubercular areas have been set up, and the minister told us a few nights ago that there are more veterinaiy surgeons employed than ever before, and more is being done for that work.
In the light of those facts, this rate of condemnation insurance should be lighter. I do not want to put the figures on the record again, because I have already done so. An enormous amount of money is taken in in a year; and the amount becomes very large when it is taken for the number of years the provision has been operating.

The prices committee
intends to investigate condemnation insurance.
I assure the hon. member I am delighted to hear that.
