May I reaffirm my previous request to the minister that he consider the advisability of appointing a board of livestock commissioners in Canada for the purpose of regulating, controlling, assembling, transporting, grading, marketing and exporting livestock and livestock products.
I have gone into the matter of a board of livestock commissioners very fully on past occasions when I have spoken in the house, and I do not think it is necessary now for me to repeat my remarks to the minister, since

Supply-Agriculture
this subject has been before him and has been dealt with by him on different occasions.
In an earlier debate when I advocated the establishment of a board of livestock commissioners, I compared it with the board of grain commissioners. I had in mind the splendid record which the board of grain commissioners has made since its establishment in 1912. Farmers have long been convinced that a similar board to set up and maintain standards and to encourage a steady improvement in quality both of products and of stock would be of tremendous value to Canadian agriculture.
If our bacon and other livestock products are to compete successfully in major export markets, no effort can be spared to ensure that there shall be no deviation from strict standards of quality. The minister did say at that time it was the opinion of people, who should know', that the board of grain commissioners is ultra vires of parliament, and that the board exists only because of the service it renders to the farmers of western Canada.
Being a farmer, not a lawyer, I cannot discuss the legal aspects, but I know that for thirty-three years the board of grain commissioners have given satisfaction to farmers who were very much dissatisfied before the act was passed setting up that board. I am sure that there are ways and means of making a 'board of livestock commissioners a reality, and to satisfy the continuous requests of livestock producers for such a board.
The whole argument in my opinion simmers down to this, that in order to instil confidence among growers of grain, the government felt it necessary some years ago to set up a board of grain commissioners.
Hon. members will agree with me that such action has w'orked out most satisfactorily. The very same argument applies in connection with livestock, to an even greater degree, inasmuch as grain is a non-perishable product, and samples can be retained to a much greater degree than is the case with livestock products.
There is the additional argument, of course, that in respect of grain the grading which the farmer receives is carried right through to the consumer or miller, with the same standards prevailing. In the case of livestock, the grading does not carry through. The very fact that there is one set of specifications covering the grade of hog carcasses on which the farmer receives his settlement, another set of specifications covering the grade of Wiltshire sides from the packer to the meat board for export, and another set of specifications
covering the product sold by the meat board to the British ministry of food, calls for a neutral board's supervision.
In the case of the pork going into domestic consumption, the packer is allowed to wrap almost anything in the wrappers commonly accepted by the consumers as top grade. As far as I know, the government accepts no control over the latter handling. I know the minister will argue that his department has exercised some control over the portion going into export, but certainly they do not touch anything going into domestic trade, any more than from a sanitary point of view'.
Should the board be set up in the near future, I would suggest further that farmer representation on such a livestock board should be the strongest available. It is no place for political appointments. The greatest interest in the livestock industry is the interest of the men and women who produce the livestock; and it is a matter of prime importance that they be fully and adequately represented on such a board.
When the minister speaks later I would ask him to deal with the research his department has done into the causes of reductions in prices of different commodities which are subject to slumps, and I would ask him to tell us upon what the figures are based. I refer to the operations of the prices support board. Money is there made available, if prices become too low. Perhaps the minister would tell us something about this phase of the matter. I believe some observations from him would give the farmers a sense of security, when they know that they can keep on producing and that they will be looked after, so that they will not be subject to heavy loss after producing hog3 or cattle.
I shall have some questions later on but, with that exception, I have nothing to add at the present time.

Most of the discussion today has been from members from western Canada, and it has been most interesting to hear them express their points of view. I should think it would be wise, however, if the committee were to hear something from the two great provinces in central Canada.
Our problems are not exactly the same as they are in the west. Our system of farming is different. We farm 12 months of the year in Ontario, and also, I believe, in Quebec. We have heard something about the troubles of beef cattle and hog producers, and I want to tell the minister that the farmers in our part of the country would like to send cattle to the United States. We raise some good cattle in Ontario.
Supply-Agriculture

There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. I refer to the dairying industry. We have heard a lot about butter these last few months, and we have now reached the time when production is catching up with consumption and we shall not need oleomargarine. However, we have to look a little farther ahead to see what will happen next winter.
Your party is bringing in oleomargarine.
Where?
Just the other day.

It is important that we have a dairying policy which will assure that the consumers will have butter next winter. That would probably be brought about if the government got out of the butter business or made it profitable for those producing butter to produce it. I believe it was about January 17 last when a ceiling was put on butter to protect the consumer. It was possibly thought wise to do that. If that was reasonable at that time, it is only reasonable, now that we are coming into production, that a floor price be put on for the protection of the producer. What that floor price would be is probably a matter of opinion.
The floor under the price for cheese is 30 cents, with probably a cent or two more for a quality bonus. Then in Ontario two cents more is given. On that basis it would seem that a floor of at least 60 cents a pound would be the absolute bottom that should be put on butter. Unless something along this line is done, we may be facing a shortage of butter next year. A lot of work is involved in looking after a herd of dairy cows and keeping them up; it takes a lot of equipment and long hours must be put in. All this should be taken into consideration.
Surely the butter producers are not to be left at the bottom of the list as they were throughout the whole war. During the time of national emergency they were willing to accept that in order that cheese might be sent to Great Britain to fulfil our contracts. That time is now past, and it seems to me that the 50,000,000 pounds of cheese which we are exporting should not control the whole dairying structure.
We do not know what the consumer in Canada is willing to pay for butter, but I see no good reason for continuing the ceiling price at the present time. The producers throughout the country feel that they are entitled to a floor price. We are into the production season now, probably a week or two later than normal, and it would make a great

difference in our supply of butter next winter if the producers were assured now that a floor price would be put on. H a floor price is to be put on, or if the government is to stay in the butter business or get out of it, that should be made known immediately. It would be a good thing for the country if the minister could tell us tonight if there is a policy and what that policy is.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps there are sufficient members here to carry on an agricultural debate. Listening to the debate the other night and the remark made tonight by the hon. member for Calgary East has made me wonder if I have the right information regarding income tax and if some hon. members opposite have the wrong view. During the discussion the other night the hon. member for Souris and one or two others asked to be assured by the Minister of National Revenue that it was not necessary for farmers to make out income tax reports this year. That point was emphasized.
In my constituency a number of fishermen are in the same category as farmers, and I want to tell the committee that I have advised each and every fisherman to be sure and make out an income tax form, particularly if he did not have a taxable income.
I know the hon. member wants to be fair, but he is leaving the impression that I wanted to be sure that the farmer did not have to make out an income tax form.
I am being fair.

I quoted the heading and I asked the minister whether the man was supposed to make out an income tax form. I have advised every farmer in my riding to make out a return whether he had a taxable income or not.

I might have misunderstood the hon. member, but several asked the Minister of National Revenue if it was necessary. Either I have the wrong information or others have. The explanation given me is that the farmer or fisherman must make out an income tax return, whether he has a taxable income or not, if he wishes to average his income over a number of years. If he has not a taxable income this year and does not make out a return, if he has not a taxable income in 1949 and does not make out a return, should he make $10,000 or $15,000 in 1950 he would not be able to go back and average his income. He must make out a return every year to be able to do that.

Supply-Agriculture
I do not bring up this matter in order to criticize anyone; I simply thought that some hon. members may have the wrong impression. Unless a return is made out each year, the man making $10,000 or $15,000 in 1950 would have to pay an income tax on the full amount.

Just to get back again to this meat business, if I understood the Minister of Agriculture correctly this afternoon he stated that hog prices in Canada today are considerably higher than in any other country.
I did not say "considerably", I said "higher".

During the dinner
recess I looked up a pamphlet put out by the minister's department, the "Live Stock Review" of April 29, which is the last one we have. It states that the average livestock prices at Chicago for the week ending April 17, 1948, showed hogs, $22.37. I think that is for live weight. The same pamphlet shows the price of hogs at Winnipeg as $27.50. If it is a choice hog it will dress 80 per cent. I think that is a pretty fair average.
The premium goes on top of that.

Yes, there is a premium on top of that. It brings it to approximately twenty-two cents. I am not going to quibble about fractions. It would bring the price of hogs in Chicago and Winnipeg to an almost identical figure, even with the premium, because there is so little difference I will not argue about it. That is the point I wanted to make clear.
To keep the record straight for those who read it afterwards, may I say there is still the duty and the freight to pay to get it to Chicago or Minneapolis.

Certainly, but I am talking about the difference between the price on the two markets, because the producers in Canada also pay the freight to the yards. The point I am making is the net price to the Canadian farmer who markets his hogs in the yard in Winnipeg as compared with the United States producer who markets his hogs in Chicago.

To be exact, my statement this afternoon was intended to convey the idea that there was no other market where you could market your hogs and get as good a return as you could when you marketed them in Canada.

At any rate, I wanted to put these figures on the record from the minister's own department. I have put them
on for hogs, and I shall now put them on for cattle. The average was 28-38 cents in Chicago and eighteen cents in Winnipeg during that week. There is a difference of ten cents and a fraction there. Then again, if you want to go back to the United States shipping point there would have to be a cent and a half duty and whatever the freight happens to be there, but it still leaves quite a difference.
What I wanted to do was to support what the hon. member.for Calgary East said to the minister this afternoon when he finished making his statement about the quantities of meat in storage in Canada and the prices. I consider it important, in view of the statements that have been published in the press in the last few days as the opinion of his colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the chairman of the prices committee. The statements that he has been making about the meat in storage in Canada and the prices have been disconcerting to the livestock producers of Canada. Probably the Minister of National Health and Welfare has not realized how his statements may be taken; nevertheless he is a member of this government. Therefore I hope that the minister will make the statement before that committee as to meat in storage in Canada and the prices that he gave here this afternoon. If he did that it would be helpful and encouraging also to the producers of livestock throughout this country, because the two statements made by the ministers in the last few days are at variance. I hope the minister will see either that, his statement is made clear, personally through himself, or that his statement is made available to the prices committee in order to clear up that serious misunderstanding at this particular time.
There is another point I should like to mention. I do not want to get mixed up in the tractor issue that took place this afternoon, but I happen to have Hansard of May 21, 1941. This is what the minister said, as reported at page 3028:
A number of hon. members from that corner have referred to my opinion as to the use of horses or gasoline in farming. I should like to say that I have a farm in western Canada and I have never had a tractor.
That is the point he was making this afternoon. Later on, he said:
If I were dependent upon my farm for a living, as I have been at times, I certainly would not use a tractor.
I will admit that that exchange took place many years ago, and the whole situation has changed, but to keep the record straight I just wished to refer to that.
If the hon. member for Charlotte would take the trouble to read the Winnipeg

Tribune of May 5 he would have an enlightened picture of the most recent income tax returns filed by the farmers of the various provinces across Canada and the amounts paid by those farmers. They are about the last figures obtainable from the Department of National Revenue. The figures are interesting. If anybody is concerned about the number of farmers who have filed income tax returns by provinces and the amount of money they have paid per capita agricultural income by provinces he can get the information in that paper. I agree with what the hon. member was trying to get at a few moments ago. There has been a lot of confusion as to whether these farmers should or should not file a return if they were not liable for tax. I am sure that no hon. member in any group here would advise a farmer not to file a return if he should be liable at all. I have gone the other way, as I am sure other hon. members would do, and advised them that they should make a return and be on the safe side. I think they should do that. The point that I wanted to make was whether the heading on the form was a part of the law or just put there by some officials in the department in order that every farmer should file a return. I am not too clear on the matter yet, even after the answers I have received from the minister.
The point I wanted to impress upon the hon. member was that a farmer should be most careful about making out an income tax in the year in which he has no taxable income.

In view of the figures the minister put on the record this afternoon, I think it would be only fair that the figures for the intervening years should also be placed on the record. I do not know why the minister particularly chose the years he did because, as we all know, there was quite a hump in the intervening period between those years; that is, mainly 1944 and 1945. Production figures all across the board were very high, but now they are on the downward trend. The figures I am quoting with regard to livestock are taken from the Canada Year Book, 1947, page 351. This is the index number of animals on farms, and I think it is a very fair figure to use. I will not bother giving horses. Milk cows, 1939, stood at 97-4. I shall give each year in sequence. In 1940, the figures stood at 96-5; 1941, 95-9; 1942, 97-4; 1943 100-4; 1944, 103-9; 1945, 105-8 and 1946, 103-5! The high year was 1945. Other cattle, the 1939 figure is 95-1. The high year was 1945, and the figure was 137. In 1946 the figure was 131-1.

I now come to the total of all cattle. In 1939 the figure was 96-1. The high year was 1945 and the figure was 123-4. In 1946 the figure was 119-1. Sheep and lambs; the 1939 figure was 94-4. The high year was 1944, and the figure was 120-9. In 1946 it had dropped down to 109-6. Swine, in 1939 the figure was 110-8. The high year was 1943, and the figure was 206-9. The 1946 figure was 136-5.
I now come to egg production, which will be found at page 355 of the Canada Year Book, 1947. This figure is given in dozens of eggs, from 1941 to 1946. In 1941 the figure was 244,468,000 dozen. The high year was 1945; the figure was 373,952,000 dozen. In 1946 the figure had dropped to 346,841,000 dozen.
I now come to the total milk production. The 1942 figure was 17,448,590,000. The high year was 1945, with a production of 17,626,972,000 pounds. In 1946 it had dropped back to 16,937,028,000 pounds. To be fair, I believe the 1947 figure is a little higher, but the increase is small.
I now come to the figures for butter. The 1942 figure was 363,116,372 pounds. The high year was 1943 with a production of 367,116,476 pounds. In 1946 it had decreased to 325,591,000 pounds. The high year was 1943. There is an explanation for that. At that time the government asked that the farmers decrease their production of butter and increase the production of cheese. Therefore it was by government policy that that took place.
In cheese, the 1942 figure was 208,218,645. That was the high year, and in 1946 that figure had dropped to 148,060,000 pounds. There was a reason for that. It was government policy at that time to increase production of cheese and decrease production of butter, so as to supply the export market in Great Britain.
Now a word about hog production. As stated by the minister this afternoon, the production of hogs has probably increased in the first period of this year, but he expects it to decrease in September. I believe, as I have said before this session, that there was good reason for that decrease in the production of hogs, as there is good reason for the decrease in production of every farm product, as shown by these figures. One of the greatest reasons is the fear of the farmers across the country of what the price will be in the future. They do not know.
By order in council the price might be changed overnight, and it is the fear of that price change which is keeping the farmers from going ahead with production.
Another thing is income tax. For years the farmers have worked long hours, as we

Supply-Agriculture
all realize. Anyone who has worked on a farm knows it. The farmers are not satisfied to continue to work these long hours and then have the government tax them for the extra hours they put in. Labour in industry have done the same thing exactly. They refuse to work overtime when they are taxed highly for it, and you cannot blame them.
What is to be done? I do not know what the government figure on doing, but something will have to be done if they want to have production increased, because unfortunately it is going down and it will continue to go down as long as these two factors are predominant in the minds of farmers.
One suggestion I have made before and I should like to make it again. I refer to the extra time the farmer puts in. There is not a farmer in this country who does not want to bear his fair share of taxation. I am not suggesting that the farmers should not pay their fair share of income tax, but they are not allowed the exemptions which should be coming to them by reason of the fact that the farm is a family affair and not individual. So that, although the farmer's wife is now allowed pin money for her few hens, that is a mere drop in the bucket compared with the work she does on farms across the country.
I know the work my own mother has done, and I know the work many other women have done and are doing throughout the country, loading hay, taking the place of a man all summer and yet without recompense for that work. The return for the work is simply considered as one man's income. In many cases there may be, besides the wife, several children helping to earn on that farm, and there should be some means whereby that could be considered when the farmer makes out his income tax returns.
The minister said this afternoon that the price of hogs would be set in November or December this fall for next year. I say that is not good enough. If he expects production of hogs to go up it will take a long time for an increase in production if there is such a delay before the farmers know what price they will receive, because assuredly people will not go ahead and produce hogs now, with, as the only floor price in sight, that which they now have. As stated by the minister, the price for 1916 is the guaranteed price for 1949, which is S25. If the price of hogs did go down to $25 for next year, does the minister think he would get much production at that figure? That is the basis and the only basis on which the farmers can figure produe-5849-238i
tion now, because that is the only guarantee they have for 1949.
I made a suggestion before, and I make it again briefly, that the price of hogs should be set at least two years ahead, and that a minimum and a maximum price should be set at that time. At the present time the price of hogs is $36. There is no reason in the world why a floor of $30 and a ceiling of $35 should not be set for at least a year right now, or a year and a half, until the end of 1949. With a $5 spread in the price, it would leave the farmer with a $30 guarantee, and no one would worry much about that spread of $5. At the present time it is $11. The farmer would not worry particularly if he knew that he would get at least a floor of $30 for a two-year period, that price to be reviewed each year; a year ahead of production, instead of one month or two months, as the minister stated this afternoon, before the production period.
If the price is to be left until November or December this fall, we shall have trouble in getting production to the point where we can maintain the British bacon market, and I strongly urge that consideration be given, in the minister's price policy for hogs, to obtaining that minimum and maximum price as I suggest. I do not offer those figures absolutely. I give them simply as an example, suggesting that there might be a spread of $5 between the low and the high, and that figure be set for two years and reviewed each year.

I think I should say a few words, because a number of figures have been put on the record today which might lead people who do not know better to believe that farmers are making a lot of money. That statement has been made for a number of years, and there are still people who believe that the farmers are making more than many other occupational groups. The statement is certainly not correct.
A couple of weeks ago I put some questions on the order paper to find out from the government records just what the position is. I asked for information with respect to the number of farmers operating farms in each province during the years from 1930 to 1947 inclusive, and also during the same period the net farm income in each province each year.
I did this so that we should have figures dealing with the poor years and with some of the better years. Unfortunately we have not been able to get figures for the period 1930 to 1937 inclusive, but we have been able to get figures for the better years from 1938 to 1947 inclusive.
Supply-Agriculture

As an indication of the condition of agriculture during the depression years, tvhat many people call the hungry thirties, I have in mind a figure given from government sources some time ago of one year which I believe was one of the poorest, 1932. The average net income per farm in Canada for that year was 8198. It has been pointed out by the hon. member who has just taken his seat that that is not the income for just one individual because, as he rightly pointed out, the farmer's wife and family and hired help must get a share of that net income.
In making this calculation I have not been able to get an accurate statement, because 1931 and 1941 are the only years for which the government has been able to give the number of occupied farms. In 1931 the number of occupied farms was 728,623, and in 1941, 732,832. For my purpose I felt that an approximate figure could be obtained by taking, as an average, 730,000 occupied farms, and taking that figure I find that for the year 1938 the average net income for the farmers of Canada was $530; for 1939, $664; 1940, $725; 1941, $818; 1942, $1,513; 1943. $1,356; 1944, $1,680; 1945, $1,343; 1946. $1,590; and for 1947, the highest average of all, $1,725.
For the ten-year period that gives us a net income for each farmer in Canada of $1,194. This may be of interest to some who have not had an opportunity to get figures on farm
income. But again I point out that that is the net. income for 'the farmer, his wife and family and hired help, because they all work on the farm. I might also point out that the average farmer in Canada works not less than twelve hours a day, and in the harvest and threshing seasons, particularly in the prairie provinces, we have to work sixteen or seventeen hours a day. You might compare that with the forty-four hours a week enjoyed by many industrial workers and the forty-hour week enjoyed by other industrial workers. You might compare it also with what many people are aiming at today, the five-day working week. The farmer has no five-day or six-day week; he works seven days a week, and by working long hours of overtime it may run up to nine or ten days in a week. If the committee is willing I should like to place this table on Hansard. It is a return which was tabled only yesterday and gives the number of farmers in each province all across Canada in 1931 and 1941, and gives also the net income of the farming population in each province all across the dominion.

I think that table will be found enlightening and help to explain why the farmers of Canada are not paying more income tax than they are at the present time. I might point out that, in view of the losses the farmers suffered during the period from 1930 to 1941 particularly, some system should be worked out whereby they can make up some of their losses during that period when it comes to paying income tax, especially when it is remembered that the farmers received much less for their production during the war years than they could have if another system had been in effect. I am not going to say any more at this time, but I felt that these figures should be placed on the record to head off some false impressions that might have been given by other figures placed on the record during this discussion.

I understood the minister to say that certain classes of cattle were selling in the United States for twenty-two cents a pound and that comparable classes of cattle were selling in Canada for sixteen cents a pound, or a difference of six cents a pound between the two countries. During the dinner recess I looked up the market reports to verify the minister's figures. I could not find today's or yesterday's paper, but I got Wednesday's paper and I should like to quote Wednesday, and then ask the minister to explain the figures he gave this afternoon. On the Toronto stock market weighty steers
brought $17 to $18.50; butcher steers sold for $16.50 to $18.50, heifers, $17.50, and fed yearlings, $16.75 to $19. Butcher cows sold at from $11 to $16.
On the Chicago market Colorado fed steers brought $31.75; good and choice yearlings, $28 to $31; good and choice heifers, $27 to $31; beef cows, $19.50 to $24; sausage bulls, $24.50. The last figure is not very clear, and it may be $21.50. I cannot see any prices quoted to support the figure the minister gave of twenty-two cents on the United States market as compared with sixteen cents for the same class of cattle on the Canadian market-

The statement which I gave this afternoon was a quotation from a report of the prices committee. They took evidence from Mr. George Ross, who is quite a large operator, with a ranch in Alberta, and who, until recently, operated a ranch in Montana. He is therefore familiar with prices on both sides of the line. He gave evidence to the effect that you cannot make a comparison between any Canadian-fed cattle and corn-fed cattle on the Chicago market, that we have not comparable cattle being delivered on this side of the line. But he said that the grass-fed cattle off the ranch in Montana were comparable with the grass fed cattle in Alberta. There can be no question about that because there is only an imaginary line between Montana and Alberta. He said that that type of cattle sold on the United States market when he was before the com-

mittee about two weeks ago, at twenty-two cents a pound, and that the same grade of cattle on the Canadian market brought sixteen cents. I know that if you take the newspaper reports for cattle prices in the United States and Canada, unless you are familiar with the types of cattle that go on the United States market and the market here, it is difficult to make a comparison in prices. But this man is an expert on ranch cattle, and he said that was the comparison in prices brought by Montana and Alberta cattle.
Does he call grass-fed cattle those cattle coming off the ranches now?

I am not going to try to tell the hon. member what he was talking about, but he was giving evidence before the committee, and I think some members of this committee were present when he was giving his evidence and will bear out that that was the evidence he gave. I am not going to discuss what he may have had in mind, or anything like that. Everyone who knows George Ross knows he understands cattle and has probably sold more cattle on the United States market than most Canadians. He has had a ranch on both sides of the line, and I would take his word in regard to prices of cattle, particularly in view of the fact that he has been one of the chief advocates of getting cattle back into the United States market ever since that market was lost.

Before this item carries, I wish to say something about what has happened to the farmer in the last year, and I hope the minister will see that it does not happen again. In the last couple of weeks I have tried to understand the minister's point of view and the workings of his department; and I want to take this opportunity to compliment the minister on the efficiency of his department. I do not think any other department of this government is so well organized or equipped to give such service as the Department of Agriculture. I found that I could trace through the acreage of every crop, the production figures, the income tax paid by farmers, the marketing and practically everything but the policy of the government. I have bales of stuff. It was a fascinating experience; in fact I think the minister's performance is always fascinating.
But while I understand his department a great deal better, I must confess that I still do not understand the minister. Today we have an almost unlimited demand for every-

thing we can grow; we have good prices; yet I am afraid that we have done a great deal to discourage production and to make it hard for farmers to remain in the business and produce the animal products necessary for our export market. I am going back to 1946, when a conference was held in Ottawa on December 3, 4, 5 and 6, attended by the deputy ministers of all the provinces, representatives of the federal Department of Agriculture, officials of the United Kingdom and the United States and representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, representing the industry all across Canada. There were the representatives of agriculture, there were the representatives of all governments in Canada; there were the representatives of our potential market, representatives of the United States and the United Kingdom.
Evidently they had an excellent conference, and I agree with all their findings. I think they said some useful and sensible things, and I believe their conclusions were valid. I only wish the minister had been permitted to carry out the decisions of that conference. I believe his next job must be to organize the government so that it will have a little understanding of the needs of agriculture, because I am sure, if the minister had been permitted to carry out the decisions of that conference, agriculture today would not be resenting the things that happened last year, and would not be wondering how to plan for the coming year, and the year after that.
For instance, this conference decided that there was a great need for animal products, and that their production depended upon feed. They recognized the relationship between the price of wheat and the price of barley, and that if that relationship were upset people would divert their land to the growing of wheat and would deprive the country of its feed supply. They saw that if the price of barley went too high the feeder in the east could not afford to buy it; and they saw also that if it went too high in the west the farmer would sell his pigs and market his barley. Therefore they said the thing to do was to stabilize the farmer's costs by giving him an acreage bonus, which would help give him the cost of production but would keep down the price of feed to the eastern farmer and maintain this flow of barley so that we could maintain our over-all production. They said, too-and I think this is extremely important -that the future of Canadian agriculture on the British market depends upon our living up to the present contracts.
That is so true. As long as I can remember anything, I can remember my father, who was

Supply-Agriculture
active in farmers' organizations, worrying about how we could get the British market away from the Danish producers. The Canadian farmer has always hoped that some day we shall have a chance to compete with Denmark in the field of bacon. Here we had a marvellous opportunity to keep what we had obtained because the world was hungry. So all those attending that conference agreed on this very good program.
Then the Canadian Federation of Agriculture met and drew up their production in line with the decisions of that conference. Their objective, too, was to bring about an increase in hog production; and it was recognized that these relationships would have to be maintained. They recommended the $5 per acre bonus, that the 15-eent barley equalization payment be discontinued, that any increase in the price of barley would be prejudicial to an increase in hog production, and so on.
We all remember that last year at about this time there were severe floods in the east. This year the floods are in the west, but last year it was the east. Hon. members will remember, as I remember so well, that the farmers of Ontario were almost going crazy at that time wondering whether or not they would get in their crops, and many of them never did. So the federation of agriculture had a meeting on June 12 to draw to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture the critical feed situation resulting from these weather conditions. Here are the things they recommended when their delegation came to see the minister at that time. They recommended that the present price structure on feed grains be continued until at least July 1, 1948; that plans be made as early as possible for the movement of the normal supply of feed grains into eastern Canada and British Columbia; that, in view of the emergency in eastern Canada, special measures be instituted to move the necessary additional supplies of feed grain from the west to the east before freeze-up; and they also warned the minister that, unless extraordinary measures such as these were taken, the Canadian consumer would suffer shortages of some farm products and face the danger of high prices in connection with other products, and further that Canada would fall down badly on her export commitments.
The minister replied to the federation of agriculture and assured the delegation that a close watch was being kept on the situation; that measures would be considered to ensure the transportation of as much feed grain as -could be obtained from the west, and that, with
respect to the price and drawback situation, the minister would discuss the matter with his colleagues in the cabinet.
In reply the delegation emphasized that livestock feeders faced not only a shortage of feed but increased costs of production on two scores; and these were the factors entering into those increased costs of production. They said that, because of the late and depleted sowing program, they would have to buy extra supplies of feed, and that cancellation of the drawbacks would substantially increase the price of coarse grains.
To come further into this disastrous year for agriculture, in the fall the packer's strike developed and, as I have said before in this house, those of us in the west who were planning to ship livestock found that we had no cars. We find that, while the packers had meat for sale all the time the strike was on, they ceased taking deliveries; so our livestock could not be shipped. Finally, when the strike was settled livestock yards were glutted; at every little shipping point stockyards were full of stock and people were waiting for cars to move the cattle out.
But this was a harvest for the packing plants of the country, because this glutted condition permitted them to get their meat for less, and they were able to fill up their empty abattoirs with comparatively cheap meat. Then the government took the ceiling off coarse grains, with the result that immediately the meat people said, "The cost of feed has gone up; so, of course, meat is up"; and the consumer immediately began to pay higher prices.
What happened then? The federation of agriculture again spoke for the farmers. In their newsletter of November 7, 1947, they quote the president, Mr. Hannam, as follows:
"Nothing that has happened in Canadian agriculture in many years has stirred the farmers throughout the dominion to such resentment."
After pointing out the heavy increase in feed costs resulting from the action of the government in cancelling ceilings and subsidies, he continued:
"Furthermore the government's action has cut the feet out from under the best livestock program we ever had in Canada, which not only achieved the greatest production of livestock, dairy and poultry products in our history, but what is more important, established some degree of stability in the whole agricultural program, offering hope for some permanency for this stability in the future.
"That program has been tossed out of the window, with the marketing of oats and barley thrown back into the field of gambling on the grain exchange, and feeders of livestock not knowing where they are at in the cost of these grains."
At that time I remember that when we came back last fall it was insinuated in the house
Supply-Agriculture

that the western farmers had withheld their deliveries of grain, expecting this action on the part of the government. However, the federation of agriculture contradicts that statement, and I am glad it did because the western farmer was not guilty of that action. This is what the federation of agriculture, which speaks for all Canada, had to say on that point:
Prior to, and following the announcement of the dominion government of the removal of the ceiling prices and subsidies on oats and barley, charges were made in certain quarters that farmers in the western provinces were deliberately holding back delivery of oats and barley in the expectation of the removal of the ceilings and consequent higher prices for these grains.
Figures for farmers' marketings of these grains since August 1 completely refute these charges. These figures show, according to the dominion government report of October 23, that:
A total of 25,922,000 bushels of oats had been delivered to market by farmers, compared with 29,771,000 bushels in the same period of last year, and a total of 31,906,000 bushels of barley had been taken to market by farmers this year compared with only 29,196,000 bushels in the same period of last year.
Hear, hear.

I appreciate very much the applause.
It appears, therefore, that in 1947 the farmers had marketed slightly more barley- not less-than they had the year before. There was no evidence at all to suggest that western farmers were holding out on those in the east who needed grain.
Again in December the federation of agriculture spoke. I suggest that the minister should heed the voice of organized agriculture. This is what the president of the federation of agriculture suggests:
The question we have to decide in agriculture now is whether or not we are going to have a stabilization program for agriculture, or whether
we shall throw our industry upon the uncertainties of a free market.
And in closing, he said:
I have never known a time when all livestock farmers, including dairy and poultry producers were so upset, discouraged and bewildered.
What effect did this have upon our deliveries? I think we should ask this question: Were we able to live up to the contracts we signed with the United Kingdom? As I said earlier, the conference called in December pointed out that the future of Canadian agriculture depends upon our living up to our contracts. To what extent did we live up to the contracts we had agreed to honour?
On December 11 a return was tabled, showing our commitments. In bacon and hams our contract called for 350,000,000 pounds, and up

to November we had delivered 168,000,000 pounds. It was estimated that we would have an additional 81,000,000 pounds, or a total of
250.000.	000 pounds. So that in bacon and hams we were 100,000,000 pounds short.
On our beef agreement we had contracted for 120,000,000 pounds. It was estimated that we would be able to deliver about 36,000,000 pounds, or very little more than a quarter of what we had promised to deliver.
In respect of cheese we had promised
125.000.	000 pounds, and it was estimated that we would be able to deliver 57,000,000 pounds, or a little more than a third.
The only contracts we met were those of evaporated milk, dried skim milk powder, and eggs. I believe that is a pretty good appraisal of what happened to agriculture last year. That is not information we can afford to ignore, as a nation. And this afternoon when someone suggested-I believe it was the minister-that our deliveries of hogs had exceeded our anticipated deliveries, and someone else suggested that probably breeding stock was going on the market, I think they were right.
In that part of the country from which I come I know people are saying that there is no use staying in pigs. They believe this is a time to sell their breeding stock and their barley. I plead with the Minister of Agriculture to give us some stability, not only in contracts that we are to fill, but stability in the price of feed. We have already passed a bill which would have brought oats and barley under the control of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I am afraid it is too late now to get complementary legislation in the legislatures. Saskatchewan is the only province where such legislation has been passed. We are still waiting on Alberta and Manitoba, and I doubt very much if it will come into effect next year.
How can the farmer in the east or the west plan his production? How can we meet our commitments unless we have a long-term plan and stability?
The conference which met in December of 1946 had this to say:
Individually, it was difficult for the farm industry to assemble food products in volume and provide continuity of supply of standard quality. Bulk purchase of imports by the government would continue in the United Kingdom and some other countries for some time at least, and it was felt that a central authority in Canada could best deal with the government of another country.
It suggests that it was only by an integrated agricultural program developed for the whole of Canada, and based broadly on greater production of feeding grains in the west to supply the needs of livestock producers

Supp ly-A griculture
throughout Canada, and particularly in the eastern provinces, that progress could be made.
That is the whole picture. It shows a necessity for integration, for stability and for planning; and that for more than a month or two months or a year.
I do not need to tell the minister anything about agriculture, because no one knows more about it than he, but I would remind him that you cannot sell your breeding stock and then get back into business next year. It takes years to build up a herd of cattle, and you must make an investment in buildings, equipment, plant, land and machinery. You cannot be in this year and out next year, because your cost of production goes on in the form of interest, taxes and maintaining yourself on the farm.
I plead with the minister to work on the cabinet and try to get them to have the wheat board give us a fixed price or to establish a proper relationship between feed and prices based on contracts made with governments through our government, which is the proper mechanism to use. As individual producers we are helpless, we are defeated, we are absolutely impotent. Government is the instrument that civilization has developed to serve the needs of the community, and there is no reason why we should not use it.
I commend the minister for this kind of conference, for this kind of program and for the work of his department, and I hope that he will use it as we know he can if he can get the co-operation of his party.
I asked the minister one or two questions, but he has not had a chance to answer them. One was in connection with dairy products and butter, particularly as to a floor price.

There has been some discussion of the possibility of having a floor price under butter this year. The dairy association of Canada met me some two or three weeks ago and made certain proposals, and the advisory committee on food which meets periodically met since that time and also made certain representations. I have the matter under consideration at the moment and intend to make some representations to the government with regard to it, but up to the present I have not had an opportunity of doing so and therefore cannot give any further information at the moment.
